parts.question: Polytopes in two dimensions are known by this word. This type of shape has straight sides that enclose a figure, with no curved sides or gaps in the perimeter allowed. Triangles and quadrilaterals are examples of these shapes.

parts.label: B
parts.question: The simplest polygon is a triangle; in three dimensional space, this pyramid-shaped solid with four triangular faces is the simplest polytope.

parts.label: C
parts.question: The square and cube are analogues of each other in two- and three-dimensions, respectively. This shape is the four-dimensional analogue of the square and cube.
parts.answer: hypercube (accept tesseract; accept octachoron; accept octahedroid, but do not accept “octahedron”)

parts.label: L
parts.question: This composer worked with librettist Lorenzo Da Ponte to write operas about a womanizer who is dragged to hell by a statue and two young men who try to test their fiancees’ faithfulness. For ten points each,

parts.label: A
parts.question: Name this Austrian child prodigy. This composer worked with Da Ponte on the operas Don Giovanni and Cosi fan tutte [koh-see fon too-tay].
parts.answer: Wolfgang Amadeus Mozart (accept Johannes Chrysostomus Wolfgangus Theophilus Mozart)

parts.label: B
parts.question: With Da Ponte, Mozart also wrote an opera about this barber from Seville, who becomes a servant in Count Almaviva’s house and is engaged to Susanna.
parts.answer: Figaro (accept The Marriage of Figaro; accept Le nozze di Figaro; do not accept or prompt on “The Barber of Seville”)

parts.label: C
parts.question: After splitting with Da Ponte, Mozart worked with Emanuel Schikaneder to write this opera, in which the Queen of the Night sends her daughter, Pamina, to kill the priest Sarastro.

parts.label: L
parts.question: This writer describes woods that are “lovely, dark, and deep” and a choice between two equal paths in two of his poems. For ten points each,

parts.label: A
parts.question: Name this American poet who wrote “Stopping By Woods on a Snowy Evening” and “The Road Not Taken.”

parts.label: B
parts.question: In a poem about “Mending” one of these structures, Frost describes the natural forces that disturb one of these structures between his property and his neighbor’s.
parts.answer: wall (accept Mending Wall; do NOT accept or prompt on “fence”)

parts.label: C
parts.question: In another poem, Frost uses two specific words to describe the forces of “desire” and “hate,” both of which hold the power to destroy the world. Give either word, which both appear in the title of the poem.
parts.answer: fire OR ice (accept either term; accept Fire and Ice; do NOT accept or prompt on similar terms like “flame” or “water”)

parts.label: L
parts.question: The building of one of these structures would have doomed the Abu Simbel temples built by Ramesses II, so the archaelogical sites were moved to higher ground. For ten points each,

parts.label: A
parts.question: Name this type of engineering project, such as the aforementioned Aswan example, that can generate hydroelectric power or create a reservoir for irrigation.

parts.label: B
parts.question: The Aswan High Dam is on the Nile River in this country, north of Sudan.

parts.label: C
parts.question: The Aswan High Dam created an artificial lake named for this man, who co-led the 1952 Egyptian Revolution, served as President of Egypt for the entire decade of the 1960s, and ordered the dam’s construction.

parts.label: L
parts.question: This scale is an ordinal, not nominal, scale because its values of 1 through 10 mean essentially nothing beyond their ordered ranking. For ten points each,

parts.label: A
parts.question: Name this scale that uses quartz and topaz as the references for its values of 6 and 7.
parts.answer: Mohs scale of mineral hardness (prompt on “hardness (scale)”)

parts.label: B
parts.question: The highest value on the Mohs scale, 10, is given to this valuable gemstone. This allotrope of carbon was the hardest natural material at the time of the scale’s creation.

parts.label: C
parts.question: Soapstone is made out of this easily-powdered mineral, the softest on the Mohs scale.

parts.label: L
parts.question: In this religion, male priests called houngans and female priests called mambos communicate with spirits like Papa Legba and Baron Samedi. For ten points each,

parts.label: A
parts.question: Name this religion with branches from Haiti and Louisiana that doesn’t really use effigy dolls to cast curses and control people.
parts.answer: Voodoo (accept Haitian Vodou or Louisiana Voodoo; accept Vodu or Vodun)

parts.label: B
parts.question: In Voodoo, houngans and mambos help humans use spirits called lwa [loh-ah] to communicate with this supreme god, whose name is derived from the French for “good god.”

parts.label: C
parts.question: In Voodoo, high-ranking houngans and mambos use the ason, one of these objects wound around with rainbow-colored beads, which is shaken to make noise during ceremonies.

parts.label: L
parts.question: This man argued that modern society has simplified class struggle from a complicated system of subordination into a world with one ruling class, the bourgeoisie [boorzh-wah-ZEE]. For ten points each,

parts.label: A
parts.question: Name this German philosopher who co-wrote The Communist Manifesto with Friedrich Engels.

parts.label: B
parts.question: The Communist Manifesto ends by noting that the adoption of communism would require the forceful overthrow of society’s status quo. Even so, these people, who are oppressed by the bourgeoisie, “have nothing to lose but their chains.”
parts.answer: proletarians (accept proletariat; accept proletarier or proletarierin; prompt once on answers like “laborer” that don’t use the underlined term)

parts.label: C
parts.question: After writing The Communist Manifesto, Marx worked on a four-volume treatise on this concept, the namesake of the economic system of 19th century Europe and modern America.
parts.answer: capital (accept Das Kapital; accept capitalism and word forms thereof, like capitalist)

parts.label: L
parts.question: As a fictional character, this poet explains that unbaptized babies and virtuous pagans inhabit Limbo. For ten points each,

parts.label: A
parts.question: Name this Roman poet who, in real life, wrote the Aeneid.

parts.label: B
parts.question: The fictional Virgil guides the protagonist through nine circles of suffering sinners in this poem. This work is the first section of a longer work that describes the Catholic afterlife.
parts.answer: Inferno (accept, but do not otherwise reveal, Dante’s Inferno; prompt on “Divine Comedy” or “Divina Commedia”)

parts.label: C
parts.question: The Inferno is part of the Divine Comedy, a long poem by this Italian writer.

parts.label: L
parts.question: In the conventional thermite reaction, elemental aluminum undergoes this type of reaction. For ten points each,

parts.label: A
parts.question: Name this type of reaction in which an atom loses electrons, as contrasted with a reduction.
parts.answer: oxidation (accept oxidizing or other word forms; prompt on “redox”)

parts.label: B
parts.question: In the thermite reaction, aluminum is converted into aluminum oxide by the oxidized form of this metal element; that oxide compound is also known as rust.

parts.label: C
parts.question: The thermodynamics of the reaction can be predicted by this equation. It is normally written in terms of reduction potentials, but it applies equally well to predict the Gibbs free energy of redox reactions at nonstandard reaction conditions.

parts.label: L
parts.question: A secret program of this agency harassed and spied on hundreds of activists in the mid-20th century, as discovered when its own office was burglarized in 1971. For ten points each,

parts.label: A
parts.question: Name this US governmental agency that secretly operated COINTELPRO under, ostensibly, its purview as domestic law enforcement.

parts.label: B
parts.question: The FBI heavily spied on this non-violent activist, who co-led the Montgomery bus boycott, gave the “I Have a Dream” speech, and was assassinated in 1968.

parts.label: C
parts.question: COINTELPRO spied on many Black activist groups, including the student-led SNCC [“snick”] and this group, which formed in the wake of the Montgomery bus boycott under King as its first president. The 1968 Poor People’s Campaign was led by this group, which continues to work today.

parts.label: L
parts.question: When Charles Darwin observed one of these plants with a particularly long neck, he ascertained that there must be a moth with a nose long enough to fertilize it; the moth was eventually discovered 20 years after he died. For ten points each,

parts.label: A
parts.question: Name these plants, examples of which include orchids and daisies.
parts.answer: flowers (accept blossoms; prompt on, but do not reveal otherwise, “angiosperms”)

parts.label: B
parts.question: Using flowers and fruits to spread pollen, rather than using cones or spores, was a key evolutionary advantage that this superphylum gained over its rival gymnosperms.

parts.label: C
parts.question: Flowers really only evolved as a way of convincing birds and bees to transport pollen from the stamen to this female sex organ of a plant, which is composed of a stigma, an ovary, and a style.

parts.label: L
parts.question: After this god was murdered by his brother, Set, his body was dismembered and scattered across Egypt. For ten points each,

parts.label: A
parts.question: Name this green-skinned Egyptian ruler of the underworld.
parts.answer: Osiris (accept Usiris; accept Aser; accept Usire)

parts.label: B
parts.question: This sister-wife of Osiris collected his body parts and put him back together after Set’s attack. After temporarily reviving Osiris, this goddess gives birth to Horus.
parts.answer: Isis (accept Aset; accept Iset; accept Ase)

parts.label: C
parts.question: In some tellings of the myth, the body parts of Osiris had symbolic meaning; this part is associated with the djed column or pillar, which symbolizes stability. Egyptian mummies often had djed amulets kept near this body part.

parts.label: L
parts.question: A poem addressed “To His Excellency, [this general]” commands him to “Proceed, great chief, with virtue on thy side” during the American Revolution. For ten points each,

parts.label: A
parts.question: Name this Revolutionary War general who, in the poem, is told to lead “Columbia” to victory for “freedom’s cause.”
parts.answer: George Washington (accept To His Excellency, General Washington; accept His Excellency, General Washington)

parts.label: B
parts.question: “To His Excellency, General Washington” is by this early American poet, who was emancipated from slavery after the publication of her collection Poems on Various Subjects, Religious and Moral.

parts.label: C
parts.question: One of Wheatley’s short poems reflects “On Being Brought from” this continent “to America.” Wheatley was trafficked from this continent as a child as part of the slave trade.
parts.answer: Africa (accept On Being Brought from Africa to America)

parts.label: L
parts.question: Give the following about conservation areas in Africa, for ten points each.

parts.label: A
parts.question: An annual migration of hundreds of thousands of zebras and wildebeests takes place in this region of East Africa. The world’s largest wild lion population lives within the national park of the same name.

parts.label: B
parts.question: Just east of the Serengeti National Park is a UNESCO World Heritage Site protecting one of these geographic landforms called Ngorongoro [en-GORO-en-goro], which formed from the collapse of a volcano.

parts.label: C
parts.question: The Serengeti and Ngogongoro national parks are found in this east African country. Its capital is now Dodoma, having moved last century from its largest city, Dar es Salaam.

parts.label: L
parts.question: A Jean-Jacques Rousseau quote about brioche may be the source of a saying commonly attributed to this woman. For ten points each,

parts.label: A
parts.question: Name this queen who very likely never proclaimed “Let them eat cake”, contrary to the popular myth.
parts.answer: Marie Antoinette (accept Marie Antoinette Josephe Jeanne; accept Maria Antonia Josepha Johanna; prompt on partial answers)

parts.label: B
parts.question: Marie Antoinette and her husband, Louis XVI [16th], were executed in the wake of this revolution, which began in 1789 at the Bastille prison complex.

parts.label: C
parts.question: Marie Antoinette married Louis while he held this position, the heir apparent of pre-Revolutionary France. This term is the French name of an animal that appears on the coat of arms used by its holder.

parts.label: L
parts.question: Give the following about rotational physics, for ten points each.

parts.label: A
parts.question: An object’s rotational motion can be changed by this quantity, the rotational analog of a force. Because a lever can cause an object to move around an axis, it applies this kind of twisting force.

parts.label: B
parts.question: A moving object has this quantity, which is computed by multiplying its mass and its velocity. If the object is rotating, it has the angular type of this quantity, which is calculated similarly: moment of inertia times angular velocity.

parts.label: C
parts.question: While spinning at over 1,000 RPM, this piece of lab equipment can separate plasma from the rest of the blood. You can answer with either the name of the device or the similarly named fictitious force on which it relies.
parts.answer: centrifuge (accept word forms like centrifugation; accept centrifugal force; do not accept or prompt on “centripetal (force)”)

parts.label: L
parts.question: This novel’s frame story is a letter written from Arctic ship captain Robert Walton to his sister, telling her about an encounter with two strange men. For ten points each,

parts.label: A
parts.question: Name this novel by Mary Shelley in which the title scientist describes being terrified by a humanoid “monster” he creates in his lab.
parts.answer: Frankenstein (accept, but do not otherwise reveal, Frankenstein or The Modern Prometheus)

parts.label: B
parts.question: Frankenstein is subtitled for the “Modern” version of this mythical Greek figure, since Doctor Frankenstein introducing a dangerous scientific advancement to humanity is similar to this Titan giving humans fire.

parts.label: C
parts.question: Victor Frankenstein’s meddling with forces he doesn’t fully understand causes him to abandon his creation, who becomes bitter and murders this woman, Frankenstein’s wife.
parts.answer: Elizabeth Lavenza (accept Elizabeth Lavenza; prompt on “Mrs. Frankenstein”)

parts.label: L
parts.question: Give the following about colleges whose athletic conference memberships make absolutely no sense, for ten points each.

parts.label: A
parts.question: The Big Ten is traditionally a midwestern conference, so the definition of “Midwest” officially expanded to include California in 2022 when two schools pledged to join the Big Ten. Name either school, each of which has “California” in its name.
parts.answer: University of Southern California (accept USC; prompt on “Bruins”; do not prompt on any partial answers) or University of California, Los Angeles (accept UCLA; prompt on “Bruins”; do not prompt on any partial answers)

parts.label: B
parts.question: Most of the full member schools of the Atlantic Coast Conference are at least close-ish to the coast of the Atlantic Ocean, but not all. The biggest offenders are the Cardinals of this university in north-central Kentucky.

parts.label: C
parts.question: The Atlantic 10 Conference - which actually has 15 member schools - doesn’t know where the ocean is, either. The conference includes the University of Dayton in this non-Atlantic state, as well as two schools farther west - Loyola University Chicago and Saint Louis University.

parts.label: L
parts.question: Answer the following about American sculptor Edmonia Lewis, who depicted an old man teaching a young child in the sculpture Old Arrow Maker, for ten points each.

parts.label: A
parts.question: Sculptures like Old Arrow Maker and Minehaha were inspired by Edmonia Lewis’s one-quarter heritage from this American ethnicity.
parts.answer: Native American (accept indigenous Americans; accept American Indian; accept Mississauga; accept Mississauga-Ojibwe)

parts.label: B
parts.question: Edmonia Lewis stunned the attendees of the Centennial Exposition in 1876 with her sculpture The Death of this Egyptian queen, who killed herself with an asp after the death of Mark Antony.

parts.label: C
parts.question: In another sculpture, Lewis depicted this biblical woman folding her hands in prayer as an empty water jug sits at her feet after she was sent into the desert with her son Ishmael.

parts.label: L
parts.question: The last words of this man, “I [...] am now quite ceratain that the crimes of this guilty land will never be purged away but with blood.”, were printed as a rallying cry in numerous abolitionist newspapers. For ten points each,

parts.label: A
parts.question: Name this man who was hanged for treason after carrying out a raid on a federal arsenal at Harpers’ Ferry.

parts.label: B
parts.question: The Pottawatomie Massacre took place in this state, which was said to be “Bleeding” from the sheer quantity of slavery-related rioting that took place before the Civil War.

parts.label: C
parts.question: The Pottawatomie Massacre took place three nights after pro-slavery forces sacked this Kansas town, destroying the printing capabilities of two anti-slavery newspapers and accidentally killing one man. William Quantrill later raided this town during the Civil War.

parts.label: L
parts.question: This unfortunate literary orphan is apprenticed to an undertaker and falls in with a gang of pickpockets in a novel named for him. For ten points each,

parts.label: A
parts.question: Name this Victorian boy who asks for gruel by saying, “please sir, I want some more” while living in a poor house.

parts.label: B
parts.question: Oliver Twist is by this English author, who also wrote about poor children in Great Expectations.
parts.answer: Charles Dickens (accept Charles John Huffam Dickens)

parts.label: C
parts.question: Oliver goes to work with Fagin’s gang of young pickpockets when he is recruited by this boy, whose real name is Jack Dawkins.
parts.answer: The Artful Dodger (accept Jack or Dawkins before “Jack” is read)

parts.label: L
parts.question: Many old molecular biology labs are equipped with these devices to sterilize a workspace before doing cell culture. For ten points each,

parts.label: A
parts.question: Name these devices that provide an open flame in a laboratory. They were invented by and named for a German chemist.

parts.label: B
parts.question: Bunsen burners are fed by this fossil fuel, which is mainly composed of methane but is tainted with small amounts of sulfides so that it can be smelled.

parts.label: C
parts.question: The safe way to heat a metal under a Bunsen burner is to place it in one of these round porcelain containers, which are extremely heat-resistant. A common lab demo involves measuring the weight of one after burning a magnesium ribbon.

parts.label: L
parts.question: One member of this group, Wang Hongwen, killed two of the guards attempting to arrest him; otherwise, the downfall of this group was proclaimed as bloodless. For ten points each,

parts.label: A
parts.question: Name this group of Chinese Communist Party officials whose influence peaked during the Cultural Revolution.
parts.answer: Gang of Four (accept Si ren bang)

parts.label: B
parts.question: One of the Gang of Four, Jiang Qing [jaang ching], was the widow of this Chairman of the Chinese Communist Party. The Gang of Four were arrested in October 1976, a month after this man’s death.

parts.label: C
parts.question: During the Cultural Revolution, students wearing this color of armband formed a paramilitary group that was embraced by Mao, then shunned as they became too left-wing. A collection of sayings by Mao was published in a “Little” book of this color.
parts.answer: red (accept Red Guard; accept Little Red Book)

parts.label: L
parts.question: In the Quran, this religious figure is shocked to see the wise man al-Khidr cut a hole in a boat, kill a young man, and rebuild a wall. For ten points each,

parts.label: A
parts.question: Name this man who learns about the will of Allah from al-Khidr and who, in the book of Leviticus, receives numerous holy laws from Yahweh.

parts.label: B
parts.question: Before receiving the laws outlined in Leviticus, Moses receives this short set of rules from Yahweh while atop Mount Sinai. These rules include the directions not to kill and not to commit adultery.
parts.answer: Ten Commandments (accept Decalogue; accept Aseret ha’Dibrot; prompt on “Commandments” or “Dibrot” alone)

parts.label: C
parts.question: Earlier in his life, Moses follows Yahweh’s instructions to part and then close this waterway while he leads the Israelites out of Egypt.
parts.answer: Red Sea (accept Yam Suf; accept hayyam ha’adom; accept al-Bahr al-Ahmar)

parts.label: L
parts.question: Give the following about the 2022 winners of the Fields Medal, the highest honor in mathematics, for ten points each.

parts.label: A
parts.question: Hugo Duminil-Copin is a French mathematician who specializes in applying this field of math to physics. Statisticians often apply the results of this branch of math, in which the likelihood of an event is studied and given a value between 0 and 1.

parts.label: B
parts.question: Ukraine’s Maryna Viazovska, the second woman to win a Fields Medal, solved the optimization problem of packing these shapes in eight-dimensional space and in 24-dimensional space. In 3D, the volume of these shapes equals four-thirds times pi times their radius cubed.

parts.label: C
parts.question: English number theorist James Maynard built on Yitang Zhang’s study of twin primes, which are pairs of prime numbers that differ by this value.

parts.label: L
parts.question: The United States claimed victory in the Space Race because we got to the Moon, so all of these other Soviet firsts don’t really count. For ten points each,

parts.label: A
parts.question: This first artificial satellite to orbit Earth was launched in October 1957. It broadcast a beeping radio signal for three weeks.

parts.label: B
parts.question: In 1957, this dog was picked up off the streets of Moscow and became the first creature to orbit the Earth, flying aboard Sputnik 2.

parts.label: C
parts.question: In 1961, Yuri Gagarin became the first human in space, flying aboard this spacecraft.

parts.label: L
parts.question: A novel set in this modern country follows Saleem Sinai, who is born at the end of the British Raj. For ten points each,

parts.label: A
parts.question: Name this modern country whose 1947 independence from Britain was fictionalized in the novel Midnight’s Children, which is partially set in Mumbai.
parts.answer: India (accept Republic of India; accept Bharat Ganrajya)

parts.label: B
parts.question: This Indian-born author wrote Midnight’s Children, and was nearly-fatally stabbed in a 2022 attack.
parts.answer: Salman Rushdie (accept Sir Ahmed Salman Rushdie)

parts.label: C
parts.question: Salman Rushdie’s attack came after decades of careful living. His death was called for in 1989 because he wrote this novel, in which Gibreel Farishta and Saladin Chamcha survive the explosion of an airplane.

parts.label: L
parts.question: This man closed down a newspaper called the Independent after being sued for publishing libelous editorials that blamed Jews for violence committed against them. For ten points each,

parts.label: A
parts.question: Name this incredibly anti-semitic American industrialist. This man’s use of the assembly line greatly boosted his factories’ output of Model T cars.

parts.label: B
parts.question: The Independent was named for this Michigan town, which was Ford’s birthplace and is still the site of the River Rouge factory and Ford headquarters. Today, this city is home to America’s largest Muslim population.

parts.label: C
parts.question: Ford’s business schemes included building Fordlandia, a company town and plantation in Brazil that produced this key material for car production. The plantation failed in less than a decade, but the town has since been reclaimed by a few thousand Brazilians.

parts.label: L
parts.question: The final movement of this work, “Neptune, the Mystic”, was premiered with a choir of students from St. Paul’s Girls’ School. For ten points each,

parts.label: A
parts.question: Name this astrologically-inspired orchestral suite that opens with “Mars, the Bringer of War”.

parts.label: B
parts.question: This English composer, who taught at St. Paul’s and was thus able to arrange the choir on very short notice, composed The Planets.

parts.label: C
parts.question: Holst’s suite includes seven movements. He omitted Earth for astrological reasons, and he omitted this dwarf planet because Clyde Tombaugh was still over a decade away from discovering it.

parts.label: L
parts.question: Some varieties of French have up to seventeen of these sounds, including the schwa [shwah]. For ten points each,

parts.label: A
parts.question: Give the linguistic term for a sound of speech made with an open vocal tract. These sounds are contrasted with consonants, in which the tract is constricted or closed at some point.

parts.label: B
parts.question: Some vowel sounds, like the “oy” in “toy,” are made up of two gliding vowel sounds; the combined sound is known by this term, from the Greek for “two sounds.”

parts.label: C
parts.question: Diphthongs are written using two symbols in this standardized alphabet, whose basic set of 107 letters and 52 diacritic symbols is used to help standardize pronunciation.

parts.label: L
parts.question: On a diagram of these systems, a resistor is indicated by a line with jagged waves, and an inductor is indicated with curls in the wire – and certainly, bad handwriting has never cause any issues with that. For ten points each, Give this term for an electrical network in which current can flow in a closed loop.

parts.label: A
parts.question: Give this term for an electrical network in which current can flow in a closed loop.

parts.label: B
parts.question: In a circuit, this device uses semiconducting material to either amplify or switch the signal. These devices allowed for the invention of small, powerful electronic gadgets - the most famous example is probably a handheld radio named for them.

parts.label: C
parts.question: This circuit element is displayed as two parallel lines causing a gap in the wire. The amount of charge that these devices can store is measured in farads.

parts.label: L
parts.question: A revolution based in this city culminated in a show trial that lasted one hour, after which the President and his wife were executed so quickly that the TV cameras couldn’t even get set up. For ten points each,

parts.label: A
parts.question: Name this Eastern European capital city. It was the home of Nicolae and Elena Ceausescu [show-CHESS-koo] until they fled amidst a 1989 anti-Communist revolution.

parts.label: B
parts.question: Bucharest is the capital of this Eastern European country.

parts.label: C
parts.question: Nicolae and Elena Ceausescu were executed on this holiday in 1989. Other historical events on this day include Mikhail Gorbachev’s resignation as Soviet President and, much earlier, Charlemagne’s crowning as Emperor of the Romans in 800 CE.

parts.label: L
parts.question: This literary character is killed by his fiancee’s husband, who is from the House of Montague. For ten points each,

parts.label: A
parts.question: Name this Shakespeare character. This count of Verona dies at the tomb of his fiancee, who is the daughter of Lord Capulet.

parts.label: B
parts.question: Count Paris is a victim of the feud between the Montague and Capulet families in this Shakespeare play about a pair of “star-cross’d lovers.”
parts.answer: Romeo and Juliet (accept The Tragedy of Romeo and Juliet)

parts.label: C
parts.question: Paris is a relative of this friend of Romeo. This man is killed by Juliet’s cousin Tybalt earlier in the play.

parts.label: L
parts.question: British television features game shows that are typically less tense than American TV. For ten points each,

parts.label: A
parts.question: The genre of relaxing reality competitions was perfected by this show, in which bakers compete in a tent each week. In the most recent 13th series, judges Paul Hollywood and Prue Leith were lampooned for their take on Mexican food.
parts.answer: The Great British Bake Off (accept GBBO; accept The Great British Baking Show)

parts.label: B
parts.question: Greg Davies and Alex Horne present this show, in which five comedian panelists struggle to complete Alex’s ridiculous assignments, such as “eat the most watermelon in one minute” or “get a camel through the smallest gap.”

parts.label: C
parts.question: In this game show, a rare instance of a British competition having a successful American spinoff, trivia experts like Victoria Groce [“gross”] and James Holzhauer attempt to catch opposing contestants, preventing them from winning any money.

parts.label: L
parts.question: Give the following about famous psychological experiments and tests, for ten points each.

parts.label: A
parts.question: In 1972, Walter Mischel studied delayed gratification by putting one of these sweet treats in a room with a child and telling them that, if they wait a small amount of time without eating it, they’ll get an extra one.
parts.answer: marshmallow (accept additional information, like marshmallow test; accept pretzel sticks; prompt on “candy”)

parts.label: B
parts.question: In a much less whimsical experiment, this professor randomly assigned volunteers as either prisoners or prison guards, then observed five days of abuse in a simulated prison before Christina Maslach convinced him to shut down the experiment.

parts.label: C
parts.question: The 1972 marshmallow test and Zimbardo’s prison experiment were both conducted by this elite private university in California, near Palo Alto south of San Francisco.

parts.label: L
parts.question: This artist created The Genius of Victory for the tomb of Julius II [second], but it was not included in the finished tomb. For ten points each,

parts.label: A
parts.question: Name this Italian Renaissance sculptor who did manage to include a scupture of a horned Moses as well as a Rebellious Slave and a Dying Slave for the same tomb.
parts.answer: Michelangelo (accept Michelangelo di Lodovico Buonarroti Simoni)

parts.label: B
parts.question: Julius II was the “warrior” one of these religious leaders. Michelangelo earned commissions from several of these leaders to produce art for the Vatican.
parts.answer: Pope (accept Bishop of Rome; accept Roman Pontiff; accept Pontifex Maximus)

parts.label: C
parts.question: Julius II commissioned Michelangelo to paint the walls and ceiling of this chapel in the Vatican’s Apostolic Palace. Michelangelo included an iconic image of God reaching toward Adam on this chapel’s ceiling.

parts.label: L
parts.question: The god Iktomi usually takes the form of this animal, and inspired the creation of hoops holding string nets that are used as protective charms for children. For ten points each,

parts.label: A
parts.question: Name these web-spinning creatures.

parts.label: B
parts.question: Iktomi appears in the religious tales of this Native American people, who make up the Sioux people with the Dakota.

parts.label: C
parts.question: Other Native American religions feature this cunning character, who is named for and behaves like a common wild canine.

parts.label: L
parts.question: The longest-serving holder of this post, John Marshall, greatly expanded its power through the policy of judicial review. For ten points each,

parts.label: A
parts.question: Name this judicial position, the leader of the highest court of the United States.
parts.answer: Chief Justice of the Supreme Court

parts.label: B
parts.question: This man succeeded Marshall as Chief Justice in 1836. This pro-slavery activist issued several rulings that President Lincoln refused to obey, and Lincoln refused to publicly acknowledge his 1864 death.
parts.answer: Roger Taney ([tawny], but be lenient; accept Roger Brooke Taney)

parts.label: C
parts.question: Taney wrote the highly controversial opinion in this 1857 case, which struck down the Missouri Compromise and ruled that African-Americans were not protected by the Constitution.
parts.answer: Dred Scott vs. Sanford (accept Dred Scott vs. Sandford)

parts.label: L
parts.question: The 2020 Nobel Prize in Physiology and Medicine was awarded to a team of researchers who discovered a surprising “C” form of this disease that is mostly caused by botched blood transfusions. For ten points each,

parts.label: A
parts.question: Name this type of inflammation whose most common forms, A and B, are due to viral infection.

parts.label: B
parts.question: Hepatitis is the inflammation of this largest internal body organ. Alcohol abuse can lead to its cirrhosis.

parts.label: C
parts.question: The tell-tale sign of liver damage is this symptom, a yellowing of the skin and eyes, due to the accumulation of bilirubin in the blood.

parts.label: L
parts.question: This novel’s protagonist is aided by Zhu Ba-jie and Sha Wu-jing, whose names are usually translated into English as Pigsy and Sandy. For ten points each,

parts.label: A
parts.question: Name this sixteenth-century novel in which Sun Wu-kong helps a Tang Dynasty Buddhist monk travel to India to get holy sutras.
parts.answer: Journey to the West (accept Xi You Ji)

parts.label: B
parts.question: Journey to the West is one of the Four Great Classics of this Asian country, where it was written during the Ming Dynasty.

parts.label: C
parts.question: In English translations of Journey to the West, Sun Wukong’s name is often translated as this animal. Sun Wukong is the “king” of these playful, ape-like animals, which have prehensile tails.

parts.label: L
parts.question: Addition and subtraction have this relationship, and negative numbers are called the “additive” form of this term because “a plus negative a” gives zero. For ten points each,

parts.label: A
parts.question: Give this technical term for “un-doing” a mathematical operation, or for the object that does the “un-doing”.
parts.answer: inverse (accept any additional information, such as “inverse operation” or “additive inverse”; accept word forms like inverting)

parts.label: B
parts.question: This term describes the multiplicative inverse of a number. Dividing 1 by a number gives this value; for example, “one-half” and “two” are this kind of number for each other.

parts.label: C
parts.question: One is the only positive number that is its own reciprocal, and this is the only positive number that is equal to “its reciprocal plus 1”. The Greek letter phi [fee] symbolizes this number, which is the ratio between the side lengths of a particularly aesthetically pleasing rectangle.
parts.answer: golden ratio (accept golden mean, cut, proportion, number, or rectangle)

parts.label: L
parts.question: According to legend, this empire’s most famous ruler gained power when his predecessor sailed a fleet of 2,000 ships across the Atlantic and never returned. For ten points each,

parts.label: A
parts.question: Name this medieval-era West African empire that was founded by Sundiata Keita and ruled by Musa I. A modern African country shares this name.

parts.label: B
parts.question: Rulers of the Mali Empire like Musa I were given this title, the Mandinka word for king or emperor.

parts.label: C
parts.question: Cities of the Mali Empire included Gao, Niani, and this trade hub. The University of Sankore was built in this city, which gained a reputation in Europe as a mysterious, hard-to-find city in the 19th century.

parts.label: L
parts.question: Two works by this poet announce “I sound my barbaric yawp over the roofs of the world” and say that a “great star early droop’d in the western sky at night.” For ten points each,

parts.label: A
parts.question: Name this American poet who frequently edited and republished his poetry collection Leaves of Grass.

parts.label: B
parts.question: Whitman wrote about his “barbaric yawp” in this long poem, in which he declares, “I celebrate myself.”

parts.label: C
parts.question: The “great star early droop’d in the western sky” in a Whitman poem named for these springtime flowers “with heart-shaped leaves of rich green” and “many a pointed blossom.”
parts.answer: Lilacs (accept When Lilacs Last in the Dooryard Bloom’d)

parts.label: L
parts.question: A primary driver of climate change is this effect, which is primarily driven by the concentration of gases like carbon dioxide. For ten points each,

parts.label: A
parts.question: Name this process in which gases in the atmosphere trap radiative heat, causing the Earth’s temperature to rise.

parts.label: B
parts.question: The greenhouse effect is stronger when the surface temperature is higher, and the surface temperature rises when the greenhouse effect increases. The greenhouse effect can thus cause this type of “loop”, in which the effect of a cause-and-effect system leads to more of the cause.

parts.label: C
parts.question: An atmospheric layer of this important greenhouse gas, which consists of three atoms of oxygen, insulates the Earth from ultraviolet radiation.

parts.label: L
parts.question: Name the following musicals with famous dance sequences, for ten points each.

parts.label: A
parts.question: This Rodgers and Hammerstein musical essentially invented the dream ballet, a sequence in which the dance advances the plot and no singing takes place, in its Act 1 finale in which Laurey realizes she loves Curly, not Jud. This musical ends with Laurey and her new husband leaving for their honeymoon in the surrey with the fringe on top.

parts.label: B
parts.question: Gillian Lynne choreographed the Jellicle Ball in this Andrew Lloyd Webber musical, whose singing roles include Skimbleshanks.

parts.label: C
parts.question: Bob Fosse’s signature jazz hands are used throughout this musical, in which Roxie Hart and Velma Kelly try to get acquitted of murder in Illinois during the Jazz Age.

parts.label: L
parts.question: Give the following about the development of frontier land in 19th century America, for ten points each.

parts.label: A
parts.question: Joseph Glidden invented an efficient form of this type of steel wire, whose jagged points kept cattle contained at a far cheaper construction cost than wooden fencing.

parts.label: B
parts.question: This term describes a lifestyle of self-sufficient agriculture and domestic life, but it may be more familiar today as the name of an 1862 act that allowed people to purchase up to 160 acres of land if they improved and lived on the land for five years.
parts.answer: homesteading (accept word forms, like homesteader; accept Homestead Act)

parts.label: C
parts.question: The government’s interference with Native American land wasn’t limited to taking it; this 1887 act allowed the government to subdivide communal land into individual allotments, thereby imposing capitalism on several tribes. The government could then buy the chunks of land left over after subdivision.

parts.label: L
parts.question: The law of mass action assumes that concentration is being measured in this format. For ten points each,

parts.label: A
parts.question: Name this primary method of measuring a solution’s concentration, which is defined as moles of solute divided by liters of solution.

parts.label: B
parts.question: Molality, on the other hand, replaces “liters of solution” with the mass of the solute measured in these units. This base SI unit is the mass of a liter of water.
parts.answer: kilogram (do not accept or prompt on “gram”)

parts.label: C
parts.question: Molality is mainly useful for solving chemistry problems if the temperature changes, since a solution’s volume increases as it heats up. For instance, it is used to calculate boiling point elevation, which is one of these properties that depend on solute concentration but not identity.

parts.label: L
parts.question: The legend of Hunahpu and Xbalanque [hoo-nah-poo and sh’bah-LAHN-kay] is the subject of one of these peoples’ oldest myths. For ten points each,

parts.label: A
parts.question: Name this Mesoamerican civilization whose myths and history are recorded in the Popol Vuh. These people built the city of Chichen Itza on the Yucatan Peninsula.

parts.label: B
parts.question: Hunahpu and Xbalanque are one of several pairs of heroes in American mythologies that have this familial relationship.

parts.label: C
parts.question: In the myth, the Hero Twins are summoned to this Mayan underworld, where they play the ball game and trick the lords of this place, One Death and Seven Death, into being sacrificed.

parts.label: L
parts.question: For a week in 2010, a volcanic eruption on this island disrupted air travel throughout Europe. For ten points each,

parts.label: A
parts.question: Name this North Atlantic island, the site of Eyjafjallajokull [AY-yuh–f’YAT-luh–YO-kull] and numerous other volcanoes, geysers, and hot springs.

parts.label: B
parts.question: Almost all of Iceland’s energy production is renewable; it has ample sources of both hydroelectric power and this type of power, generated by its hot springs and geysers.

parts.label: C
parts.question: More than half of Iceland’s population lives in this city, the northernmost world capital.

parts.label: L
parts.question: The Pied Piper of Hamelin might have begun as a child-friendly way to talk about the devastation left by this disease. For ten points each,

parts.label: A
parts.question: Name this disease that spread across Europe in the 1300s with the help of rat fleas.
parts.answer: plague (accept Black Plague; accept bubonic plague; accept Black Death)

parts.label: B
parts.question: Giovanni Boccaccio [boh-KAH-chee-oh] wrote this short story collection, in which ten young nobles gather to tell stories while fleeing from the Black Death in Florence.

parts.label: C
parts.question: In one of the stories of the Decameron, named “The Patient Griselda,” Griselda’s husband tests her suitability as a wife by claiming he has killed two people with this relationship to her.
parts.answer: her children (accept her son and daughter)

parts.label: L
parts.question: Johannes Ringk recorded the only known copy of a piece for this instrument, in which pedalboard notes are marked with a “p” instead of being written on a separate musical staff. For ten points each,

parts.label: A
parts.question: Name this enormous keyboard instrument that pushes air through arrays of metal pipes.

parts.label: B
parts.question: This composer supposedly walked 250 miles to Lubeck to hear Dietrich Buxtehude, a famous organ player. This composer also wrote the Brandenburg Concertos and numerous fugues [fyoogs].

parts.label: C
parts.question: Bach wrote many works for the organ. Johannes Ringk recorded the sheet music for Bach’s Prelude and Fugue in this minor key, which has one flat.

parts.label: L
parts.question: Sir Arthur Conan Doyle got frustrated by writing stories about this popular detective and killed him off, but ended up writing sixty works about him anyway. For ten points each,

parts.label: A
parts.question: Name this fictional English detective, who amazes Doctor Watson with his ability to solve crimes using science.

parts.label: B
parts.question: Doyle became frustrated and tried to kill Holmes off in the story “The Final Problem,” during which the detective tumbles over the Reichenbach Falls with this criminal mastermind.

parts.label: C
parts.question: After “The Final Problem,” Doyle gave in to public demand and published this novel, in which Holmes investigates a mysterious canine apparition that haunts an estate in Dartmoor.

parts.label: L
parts.question: Three of the newest US National Parks are based on sand dunes. For ten points each,

parts.label: A
parts.question: A national park is located entirely within the White Sands missile testing range in this state, near the cities of Alamogordo and Las Cruces.

parts.label: B
parts.question: The tallest sand dunes in America are in Great Sand Dunes National Park in this state. More than half of the United States’ “fourteeners” - mountains taller than 14,000 feet - are found in this Rocky Mountain state.

parts.label: C
parts.question: Indiana Dunes National Park lies on the shores of this Great Lake. Of all the states that have shoreline on the Great Lakes, Indiana’s shoreline on this lake is the shortest, and the dunes are pretty much the only thing to visit there.

parts.label: L
parts.question: Electrum is one of these materials composed of gold and silver. For ten points each,

parts.label: A
parts.question: Name this solid mixtures, usually comprised of two metals, which also include useful materials like bronze and brass.

parts.label: B
parts.question: Nonmetals can form alloys too. For example, this element is alloyed to iron in steel.

parts.label: C
parts.question: Metallurgists often alloy aluminum with this other nonmetal to make them easier to melt. Extremely pure forms of this element are often doped with aluminum, boron, or phosphorus, to increase the number of charge carriers.

parts.label: L
parts.question: Give the following about historical statues by Daniel Chester French, for ten points each.

parts.label: A
parts.question: French’s best known subject is Abraham Lincoln, but before he designed the seated statue in the Lincoln Memorial, he created an eight-foot-tall statue that stands on the grounds of this state’s Capitol building in Lincoln.

parts.label: B
parts.question: A French memorial to this man, Lincoln’s only Secretary of State, stands in his hometown of Florida, New York. Numerous statues of this man stand in Alaska, a territory he purchased from Russia.

parts.label: C
parts.question: French’s memorial statue of Gallaudet sitting and teaching Alice Cogswell stands on the grounds of Gallaudet University, the only college in the world in which all services are designed to accommodate this disability.
parts.answer: deafness (accept descriptions of a loss of hearing)

parts.label: L
parts.question: For sleeping with Poseidon in Athena’s temple, this mythical woman was punished by having her hair turned into writhing snakes. For ten points each,

parts.label: A
parts.question: Name this gorgon who could turn humans to stone with her gaze.

parts.label: B
parts.question: This Greek hero, who rescued the princess Andromeda, used a mirrored shield to slay Medusa without looking at her directly.

parts.label: C
parts.question: After Perseus killed Medusa, he took her head to Athena, who set it onto this legendary shield.

parts.label: L
parts.question: Name some quirks of plant cells, for ten points each.

parts.label: A
parts.question: Perhaps the most meaningful quirk, compared to animal cells, is that plant cells have these organelles where photosynthesis occurs.

parts.label: B
parts.question: Plant cells have a rigid wall made of cellulose, which maintains turgidity. By contrast, animal cells just have this flexible and semipermeable lipid bilayer, which lets water freely in and out.
parts.answer: cell membrane (accept plasma membrane or PM)

parts.label: C
parts.question: Although plants use cellulose in their cell walls, animals can’t make it. The closest structural polysaccharide made by animals is this polymer of N-acetyl-glucosamine, which comprises the cell walls of many fungi as well as the exoskeletons of insects.

parts.label: L
parts.question: Give the following about simplifying fractions, for ten points each.

parts.label: A
parts.question: Algebra teachers often note that it is preferred to not have square root symbols in this part of a fraction, found below the numerator. Good news if you don’t like rationalizing this part of a fraction; higher math classes often don’t care!

parts.label: B
parts.question: When a complex number is in the denominator of a fraction, you can multiply both the numerator and denominator by the conjugate of the complex number to simplify. What is the conjugate of the complex number “five plus i”?

parts.label: C
parts.question: A fraction is considered to be “in simplest terms” when the numerator and denominator have no common factors. When two numbers have no shared factors, they are said to have this property, which has two names each ending with the term “prime.” Give either name.
parts.answer: co-prime or relatively prime (accept either; do not prompt on partial answers.)

parts.label: L
parts.question: This long novel follows the fate of French citizens from the time of Napoleon to the 1832 June Rebellion in Paris. For ten points each,

parts.label: A
parts.question: Name this novel by Victor Hugo that was made into a popular musical in which the convict Jean Valjean [zhawn val-zhawn] struggles to raise his adopted daughter, Cosette.

parts.label: B
parts.question: In Les Miserables ´ , Jean Valjean lives in hiding to avoid this police inspector, who is determined to lock him up for crimes he committed in the 1790s.

parts.label: C
parts.question: This young nobleman and student joins the Friends of the ABC to fight in the June Rebellion, and falls in love with Cosette, marrying her near the end of the novel.
parts.answer: Marius Pontmercy (accept Marius Pontmercy, with both underlined parts required; prompt on “Pontmercy” alone)

parts.label: L
parts.question: Name the following brutal ancient Roman emperors, for ten points each.

parts.label: A
parts.question: This third Emperor of Rome was particularly cruel in treating his underlings and was accused of numerous insane acts, such as his plan to make his own horse a consul.
parts.answer: Caligula (accept Gaius Julius Caesar Augustus Germanicus, but do not prompt on any partial answers thereof)

parts.label: B
parts.question: This ruler ordered the death of his own mother, Agrippina, in 59 CE, five years before he supposedly “fiddled” while the Great Fire of Rome burned on.
parts.answer: Nero Claudius Caesar Augustus Germanicus (do not accept or prompt on any of the non-underlined names if given alone)

parts.label: C
parts.question: The Bar Kokhba revolt in Judea was suppressed by this emperor, who ordered the construction of a wall along the northern border of Roman Britain in 122 CE.
parts.answer: Hadrian (accept Caesar Traianus Hadrianus, but do not prompt on any partial answers thereof; accept Hadrian’s Wall)

parts.label: L
parts.question: Name some completely unrelated poems written by Edgar Allan Poe, for ten points each.

parts.label: A
parts.question: This poem’s speaker mourns his lost love, Lenore, and falls into despair when he hears the title bird repeat “Nevermore.”

parts.label: B
parts.question: This poem’s speaker mourns his lost love, the title woman, who lives “in a kingdom by the sea” until she is “chilled and killed” by jealous angels.
parts.answer: Annabel Lee (do not accept or prompt on a partial answer)

parts.label: C
parts.question: This poem’s speaker might mourn his lost love when he hears “the melancholy menace” of the title instruments, which keep “time, time, time, / in a sort of Runic rhyme” with their knells.

parts.label: L
parts.question: In the early days of the COVID pandemic, reports of a severe shortage of this commodity led to an executive order requiring processing plants to stay open. For ten points each,

parts.label: A
parts.question: Name this general type of commodity whose affected producers included Cargill, Smithfield, JBS, and Tyson.
parts.answer: meat (accept any specific kind of meat, including beef, chicken, and pork; prompt on “food”)

parts.label: B
parts.question: The national market for meat is considered an oligopoly because it’s dominated by a small number of firms. In meat’s case, that’s the “Big Five.” If a market only has one major seller, it’s described by this term instead.

parts.label: C
parts.question: The market for this product is also dominated by an oligopoly, led by Abbott Nutrition. After two infants died in early 2022, Abbott issued a recall due to bacterial contamination, and a drastic shortage of this product ensued.
parts.answer: baby formula (accept infant formula; do not prompt on “milk”)

parts.label: L
parts.question: The first of three American wars against these people took place in Spanish-controlled territory, and the second included the Battle of Lake Okeechobee. For ten points each,

parts.label: A
parts.question: Name this Native American tribe, which split from the Creek. After the second war against these people, the US forced many of them to live in the Everglades.

parts.label: B
parts.question: The Seminole Wars took place in this southern US state, which was given to the US by Spain in the Adams-Onis Treaty of 1819.

parts.label: C
parts.question: This 12th US President gained his nickname of “Old Rough and Ready” during a military career that included fighting in the Second Seminole War.

parts.label: L
parts.question: A common lesson in beginner’s optics will use a triangular one of these objects to disperse a beam of white light into a rainbow of colors. For ten points each,

parts.label: A
parts.question: Give this term for an object whose angled, transparent sides can refract light.

parts.label: B
parts.question: How much bending a light beam will undergo depends on the medium in which it’s traveling; that idea is quantified by this dimensionless number. This value is roughly 1.33 for water, almost 1 for air, and exactly 1 for a vacuum.
parts.answer: index of refraction (accept n; prompt on “index”)

parts.label: C
parts.question: Refraction is the result of a change in this quantity as a wave enters a new medium. This quantity, the distance between two crests or two troughs in a wave, is greater for red light than for blue light.

parts.label: L
parts.question: On the opening night of the 1994 Winter Olympics, a group of thieves left a note thanking the National Gallery in Oslo for having lax security. For ten points each,

parts.label: A
parts.question: The thieves stole a version of this painting, in which a swirling blood-red sky appears above a figure clasping its shocked face in its hands.
parts.answer: The Scream (accept Skrik; accept Der Schrei der Natur)

parts.label: B
parts.question: Several different versions of The Scream were painted by this Norwegian artist.

parts.label: C
parts.question: Munch’s paintings have been common targets of theft. In 1998, a version of this painting, depicting a red-haired woman embracing a man, was stolen from another museum in Oslo. Munch disputed the common supernatural interpretation of this work, claiming that the woman was simply kissing the man on the neck.

parts.label: L
parts.question: In a play by Aristophanes, these animals serve as the chorus while Dionysus rows across a lake toward the underworld. For ten points each,

parts.label: A
parts.question: Name these amphibians whose croaking is imitated by the line “bre-ke-ke-kax ko-ax ko-ax.”

parts.label: B
parts.question: Although much of The Frogs concerns a verbal battle between two tragic playwrights, The Frogs itself is a work in this genre, like most of the surviving plays by Aristophanes.
parts.answer: comedy (accept word forms like comedic plays; accept komoidia)

parts.label: C
parts.question: In The Frogs, Dionysus journeys to the underworld to bring Euripides back from the dead, but instead retrieves this tragic playwright of the Oresteia.

parts.label: L
parts.question: In the late 19th century, Giovanni Schiaparelli [skap-ah-relli] saw channels on the surface of this planet, and a mis-translation convinced some that there was liquid water running on its surface. For ten points each,

parts.label: A
parts.question: Name this fourth planet from the Sun.

parts.label: B
parts.question: Schiaparelli’s report mutated into the idea that Martians had built these structures on Mars, possibly for irrigation.

parts.label: C
parts.question: Today, we know that Schiaparelli’s canali were an optical inaccuracy, and scientists continue to look for water on Mars using equipment like this rover, which landed in 2012 and continues to operate today. The Perseverence rover joined it on Mars in 2021.

parts.label: L
parts.question: The first of this work’s 18 books is the Adi Parva, whose stories include the tale of Shakuntala, whose husband Dushyanta fails to recognize her without her wedding ring. For ten points each,

parts.label: A
parts.question: Name this ancient Indian epic poem about the civil war between the Kauravas and Pandavas. At nearly two million words, this work is considered the longest poem ever written.
parts.answer: Mahabharata (do not accept or prompt on “Bhagavad Gita”)

parts.label: B
parts.question: The most famous section of the Mahabharata is the Bhagavad Gita, a dialogue between a prince of the Pandavas and this character, the prince’s charioteer. In modern Hinduism, this revered eighth avatar of Vishnu is the subject of a mantra that also names Rama and Hare [hah-ray].

parts.label: C
parts.question: Krishna advises this third prince of the Pandavas, who is hesitant to fight until Krishna reveals his true nature.

parts.label: L
parts.question: The “ABC Powers” mediated a conference between American and Mexican diplomats in 1914. For ten points each,

parts.label: A
parts.question: The “ABC Powers” are Argentina, Brazil, and this South American country whose capital is Santiago.
parts.answer: Chile (accept Republic of Chile; accept Republica de ´ Chile)

parts.label: B
parts.question: Among the relatively few conflicts between the ABC powers is a border dispute between Chile and Argentina over this cold region of South America south of the Pampas.

parts.label: C
parts.question: Before they were the “ABC Powers”, Argentina and Brazil joined with Uruguay in the 19th century War of the Triple Alliance against this country, which lost the war decisively.
parts.answer: Paraguay (accept Republic of Paraguay; accept Republica del ´ Paraguay; accept Tavakuaireta Paraguai´ )

parts.label: L
parts.question: Answer the following about the work of American poet Maya Angelou, for ten points each.

parts.label: A
parts.question: In a poem by Angelou, a “free” one of these animals “dips his wing / in the orange sun rays / and dares to claim the sky,” while a “caged” one of the animals “sings of freedom.”
parts.answer: bird (accept the caged bird; accept the free bird; accept I Know Why the Caged Bird Sings))

parts.label: B
parts.question: In addition to the poem “Caged Bird,” Angelou also wrote the book I Know Why the Caged Bird Sings, which is one of these works. It describes her life to the age of seventeen.
parts.answer: autobiography (accept memoir; prompt on “biography;” prompt on “nonfiction”)

parts.label: C
parts.question: Angelou read another of her poems, “On the Pulse of Morning,” at the inauguration of this U.S. president.

parts.label: L
parts.question: This biologist “invented” the “auto-sexing chicken,” which apparently make it easier for breeders to classify them as male or female. For ten points each,

parts.label: A
parts.question: Name this British scientist whose important work on industrial agriculture is mostly dwarfed by his frankly self-explanatory “square” diagram that predicts the probability of how Mendelian genes are inherited.

parts.label: B
parts.question: Punnett squares are pretty useless in practice due to gene linkage, an effect first described by this American scientist. He is reviled by biologists today for his efforts in making the pesky fruit fly a model organism.

parts.label: C
parts.question: Fly-hating biologists would probably prefer to work with Punnett squares and these plants, Gregor Mendel’s favorite vegetables to study, because they are easy to see and don’t move.

parts.label: L
parts.question: Louis Farrakhan convened the Million Man March on this city in 1995, 32 years after another civil rights march on this city “for Jobs and Freedom.” For ten points each,

parts.label: A
parts.question: Name this city where Martin Luther King delivered his “I Have a Dream” speech in front of the Lincoln Memorial on the National Mall.
parts.answer: Washington, D.C. (accept DC; accept District of Columbia)

parts.label: B
parts.question: In summer 1932, an “army” of veterans marched on Washington to demand early payment of this reward for their World War I service. Herbert Hoover’s administration ordered the veterans removed by force; that didn’t exactly help his re-election campaign, but Congress did eventually make these payments early, in 1936.
parts.answer: military bonus certificates (accept Bonus Army; do not accept descriptions or synonyms)

parts.label: C
parts.question: The first group to picket the White House in DC was this movement of suffragettes, led by Alice Paul. The popular name of this group refers to their unusual protesting tactic.

parts.label: L
parts.question: The COVID pandemic created a boom in these “virtual” restaurants, such as “Pasqually’s” and “It’s Just Wings.” For ten points each,

parts.label: A
parts.question: Give this term for a restaurant that operates via delivery and pick-up, typically only via online ordering. Many of these businesses share cooking space with a real restaurant; for example, “It’s Just Wings” sells wings out of the back of a Chili’s.

parts.label: B
parts.question: Some ghost kitchen franchises aren’t tied to specific restaurants, like the burger chain developed by this YouTube star, whose real name is Jimmy Donaldson.

parts.label: C
parts.question: Scott Cawthon is developing a “Freddy Fazbear’s” ghost kitchen that will deliver this food. That’s fitting one of the earliest COVID-response ghost kitchens, Pasqually’s, sells wings and this food from within Chuck E. Cheese restaurants, which inspired the Five Nights at Freddy’s series.

parts.label: L
parts.question: In a poem about this insect, the speaker wishes for the gift “to see ourselves as others see us” and calls this bug a “crowlan ferlie.” For ten points each,

parts.label: A
parts.question: Name this parasitic insect, the subject of a poem by Robert Burns that discusses “Seeing One on a Lady’s Bonnet at Church.”
parts.answer: louse (accept lice; accept To a Louse, On Seeing One on a Lady’s Bonnet at Church)

parts.label: B
