parts.question: The title character in this “Scottish Play” conspires with his wife to murder King Duncan and briefly claim the throne of Scotland.

parts.label: B
parts.question: In this history play, the title king of England says he is “determined to prove a villain” because of the abuse he has suffered for his hunched back. He orders the death of the Princes in the Tower, his nephews.
parts.answer: Richard III [third] (accept The Tragedy of King Richard the Third; accept The Life and Death of Richard the Third)

parts.label: C
parts.question: This play’s title character, named Antonio, ends this play happily, having helped his friend Bassanio marry Portia, but he is often played as the villain for his poor treatment of the Jewish moneylender Shylock.

parts.label: L
parts.question: After the construction of the Bank of China tower, which did not follow the principles of this practice, a nearby building installed cannon-like cranes on its roof to combat its negative energy. For ten points each,

parts.label: A
parts.question: Name this long-standing Chinese practice of using classical elements and directional forces to create harmony between humans and their environment. Its name literally means “wind-water.”

parts.label: B
parts.question: Feng shui [fong shweh] attempts to balance these two forces. One is a cold, passive, feminine force, and the other is a warm, active, masculine force. They are represented as swirling black and white in a common symbol.
parts.answer: yin and yang (both underlined parts required; accept yin-yang)

parts.label: C
parts.question: Feng shui’s directional principles are tied to representations of four animals: a bird, a tiger, a tortoise, and one of these mythical creatures. These creatures are associated with rain in Asian cultures, but supposedly breathe fire in European stories.
parts.answer: dragon (accept long or lung; accept the Azure Dragon or Qinlong)

parts.label: L
parts.question: Clarence Darrow, the defense lawyer in this trial, actually told the jury “We do not see how you could” return a verdict of not guilty, as one purpose of the trial was to bring a law to a higher court. For ten points each,

parts.label: A
parts.question: Name this 1925 case, brought by the state of Tennessee against a teacher who violated the Butler Act.
parts.answer: Scopes trial (accept Scopes Monkey Trial; accept Tennessee v. John Thomas Scopes)

parts.label: B
parts.question: The Scopes Monkey Trial concerned Scopes’ illegal teaching of this scientific concept, as described by Charles Darwin and other biologists.
parts.answer: evolution of humans from other primates/apes/etc. (accept natural selection)

parts.label: C
parts.question: The prosecution’s legal team included this orator who gave the “Cross of Gold” speech, ran unsuccessfully for President three times, and was called to the stand during the Scopes trial to be questioned on the Bible.

parts.label: L
parts.question: Americans involved in this art movement included Lucy Bacon, who studied under Camille Pissarro, and Mary Cassatt, who exhibited with Edgar Degas [day-GAH] in Europe. For ten points each,

parts.label: A
parts.question: Name this 19th century art movement whose paintings were often quickly created en plein air to capture the essence of a particular setting of light.

parts.label: B
parts.question: The Impressionism movement was born in this European country, the home country of Degas and Pierre-Auguste Renoir [ren-WAHR].
parts.answer: France (accept French Republic; accept La France; accept Republique francaise)

parts.label: C
parts.question: The painting that inspired the name of the movement, Impression, Sunrise, was painted by this Frenchman. His flowing and somewhat blurry style may have partially been the result of his cataracts.
parts.answer: Claude Monet [mo-nay] (accept Oscar-Claude Monet; do not accept or prompt on “Manet”)

parts.label: L
parts.question: A carbon atom must be bonded to this many different groups for it to be chiral. For ten points each,

parts.label: A
parts.question: Give this number, which is also the number of covalent bonds that carbon atoms form in organic chemistry.

parts.label: B
parts.question: When carbon forms a double bond, it won’t be chiral, but it might still be able to form two isomers. Those isomers will be labelled with these two Latin prefixes, roughly meaning “same side” and “opposite side.”
parts.answer: cis and trans (both required; prompt on partial answers)

parts.label: C
parts.question: Most chiral molecules are centered on a carbon atom with a tetrahedral geometry and this type of orbital hybridization.

parts.label: L
parts.question: The original incarnation of this character is called at 3 AM by a man whose wife steals the phone and asks “What are you wearing?”; he responds “Uh, khakis.” For ten points each,

parts.label: A
parts.question: Name this fictional spokesman who was recast in 2020 and is now played by Kevin Miles in ads promoting the “Discount Double-Check” and other insurance products.

parts.label: B
parts.question: This Green Bay Packers quarterback and ayahuasca [aye-ah-WAHS-ka] enthusiast has appeared in numerous State Farm commercials. Indeed, this man has probably spent more time over the last several years on set with Jake from State Farm than with his estranged family.

parts.label: C
parts.question: In a 2022 State Farm Super Bowl commercial, Jake, Aaron Rodgers, and Patrick Mahomes complain about their stand-ins; Patrick Mahomes’s “lookalike” is Paul Rudd, and Jake from State Farm’s stand-in is this rapper, whose surprise 2022 album got mediocre reviews and was overshadowed by Beyonce’s surprise album a month later.
parts.answer: Drake (accept Drake from State Farm; accept Aubrey Drake Graham)

parts.label: L
parts.question: One of this man’s greatest regrets was that the Italian government rejected his application to perform in the Roman Colosseum. For ten points each,

parts.label: A
parts.question: Name this 19th century showman whose Wild West show, featuring performances from Sitting Bull and Calamity Jane, toured America and the world for decades.
parts.answer: Buffalo Bill Cody (accept William Frederick Cody)

parts.label: B
parts.question: Buffalo Bill’s finest performers included Wild Bill Hickok and this sharpshooter, who famously shot a smoking cigar from out of the mouth of her husband, Frank Butler.

parts.label: C
parts.question: In 1893, Chicago hosted one of these massive events that included the first ever Ferris Wheel. Buffalo Bill’s Wild West was denied an opportunity to perform at this event; undeterred, he brought the tour to Chicago anyway.
parts.answer: World’s Fair (accept World’s Columbian Exposition; accept World Expo; prompt on “Fair” or “Expo(sition)” alone)

parts.label: L
parts.question: This American author wrote about New England Puritans in “Young Goodman Brown,” a short story from the collection Mosses from an Old Manse. For ten points each,

parts.label: A
parts.question: Name this author, who also wrote about Puritans in The House of the Seven Gables and a novel about Hester Prynne.

parts.label: B
parts.question: In this novel by Nathaniel Hawthorne, Hester Prynne is required to sew a red “A” onto her clothes after she gives birth to her daughter, Pearl, out of wedlock.

parts.label: C
parts.question: In another short story collection, Twice-Told Tales, Hawthorne wrote this short story, in which Reverend Hooper wears a mysterious symbol of his hidden sins.

parts.label: L
parts.question: To be classified as this type of procedure, you must be guaranteed to get an output and stop the computation within a finite amount of time or steps. For ten points each,

parts.label: A
parts.question: Give this term for a set of instructions used to perform a computation. Computer programs for solving math problems are typically described by this word, but far simpler processes, long division, can be described by this word.

parts.label: B
parts.question: This British mathematician, who was prosecuted in the 1950s for being gay after years of stellar work in the war effort, is the namesake of a hypothetical machine capable of carrying out any algorithm.

parts.label: C
parts.question: Turing and the team at Bletchley Park worked on this computational task. Their greatest success was the solving of the Enigma Cipher, after which German intelligence became compromised.
parts.answer: codebreaking (accept decrypting German messages; accept deciphering German messages; accept cryptanalysis; accept word forms and descriptions thereof)

parts.label: L
parts.question: John Coltrane plays a poem, so to speak, on this instrument throughout the final movement of his album A Love Supreme. For ten points each,

parts.label: A
parts.question: Name this single-reed woodwind instrument. In a high school wind band, is typically the middle-sized member of its family.
parts.answer: tenor saxophone (prompt on “sax;” prompt on “saxophone;” prompt on “tenor”)

parts.label: B
parts.question: In smaller orchestras, a woodwind player may “double” by playing multiple saxophones, as well as this non-brass woodwind instrument. Swing musicians who focused on this instrument included Benny Goodman.

parts.label: C
parts.question: While the alto saxophone is pitched in E flat, the tenor saxophone and clarinet are each pitched in this key. Music written in this note’s major key has two flats in the key signature.
parts.answer: B flat (accept B flat major; do not accept or prompt on “B” alone)

parts.label: L
parts.question: This author wrote novels about Otto Lidenbrock, Pierre Aronnax, and Phileas Fogg in his Extraordinary Adventures series of novels. For ten points each,

parts.label: A
parts.question: Name this French author who wrote about Otto Lidenbrock taking a Journey to the Center of the Earth.

parts.label: B
parts.question: In a novel by Jules Verne, Pierre Aronnax and Ned Land are taken aboard Captain Nemo’s submarine, and travel this title distance underwater.
parts.answer: twenty thousand leagues (accept Twenty Thousand Leagues Under the Sea; accept Twenty Thousand Leagues Under the Seas; accept Vingt mille lieues sous les mers: Tour du monde sous-marin)

parts.label: C
parts.question: In another Jules Verne novel, Phileas Fogg makes a bet that he can perform this feat in only eighty days.
parts.answer: travel around the world (accept equivalents like circumnavigate the globe; accept Around the World in Eighty Days; accept Le Tour du monde en quatre-vingts jours)

parts.label: L
parts.question: Several Indian religions have a concept called dharma; in this religion, dharma is a form of righteousness taught by the 24 tirthankaras. For ten points each,

parts.label: A
parts.question: Name this Indian religion whose most recent tirthankara, Mahavira, lived over 2,500 years ago.

parts.label: B
parts.question: There are two main schools of Jainism: the “sky-clad” Digambara, whose monks have this dress code, and the “white-clad” Svetembara, who don’t. In Christianity, Adam and Eve follow this dress code before the fall of man.
parts.answer: nudity (accept nakedness; accept descriptions of not wearing clothes)

parts.label: C
parts.question: Many Indian religions include a form of this concept, in which one’s good or bad actions have a corresponding impact on one’s future. In Jainism, this concept attaches to one’s soul, either purifying it or tarnishing it.

parts.label: L
parts.question: Unlike most scientific scales that quizbowl will ask about, this one has special flags to indicate its dangerous conditions at its high end! For ten points each,

parts.label: A
parts.question: Name this scale that can extend to 17 in regions with typhooons, but typically ranges from 0, indicating calm wind, to 12, indicating winds of devastating force.

parts.label: B
parts.question: Typhoons are devastating tropical storms that occur in the western Pacific; in the Atlantic Ocean, they’re called this once they grow beyond tropical storm status.

parts.label: C
parts.question: The Beaufort scale’s value of 12 begins at this minimum wind speed, in miles per hour. On the Saffir-Simpson scale, this is the maximum sustained wind speed of a tropical storm. We’ll accept any answer within 3 miles per hour.
parts.answer: 73 miles per hour (accept any answer between 70 and 76 mph, including 70 or 76 exactly)

parts.label: L
parts.question: The Chakri Dynasty has been ruling this country since 1782, but a bloodless 1932 revolution transformed it from an absolute monarchy into a constitutional monarchy. For ten points each,

parts.label: A
parts.question: Give the modern name of this Southeast Asian country that is currently led by Vajiralongkorn [va-jee-ra-long-kon], who rules as Rama X [tenth].
parts.answer: Kingdom of Thailand (do not accept, prompt on, or reveal “Siam”)

parts.label: B
parts.question: In 1939, the country officially changed its name to Thailand from this name.

parts.label: C
parts.question: This capital city of Thailand was industrialized under Monkgut and Chulalongkorn, who ruled as kings Rama IV and V [fourth and fifth].

parts.label: L
parts.question: The financial crisis of 2008 scuttled plans to finish developing a series of artificial islands in the Persian Gulf, including one set in the shape of the world and several sets in the shape of this plant. For ten points each,

parts.label: A
parts.question: Name this tropical tree.
parts.answer: palm tree (accept Palm Islands; accept Palm Jumeirah, Palm Jebel Ali, or Palm Deira; accept Arecaceae)

parts.label: B
parts.question: Oil revenue fueled the construction of the Palm artificial islands, which lie off the coast of this most populous city in the United Arab Emirates.

parts.label: C
parts.question: Dubai’s Palm islands lie unfinished, but this tallest building in the world stands nearby and actually was completed in 2009.

parts.label: L
parts.question: Michael Feldberg argued that the Jewish sculptor Moses Jacob Ezekiel helped establish statues as a way to advance this belief. For 10 points each:

parts.label: A
parts.question: [H] Name this belief established by Alexander Stephens and supported by the Dunning School which presents the Confederacy as a “heroic defender” against Northern Aggression during the Civil War.

parts.label: B
parts.question: [M] Lost Cause supporters point to this scorched earth campaign as Northern Aggression. Savannah, Georgia was presented as a “Christmas gift” at the end of this 1864 campaign across Georgia led by William Tecumseh Sherman.
parts.answer: Sherman’s March to the Sea [prompt on Sherman’s March]

parts.label: C
parts.question: [E] Thomas Dixon Jr. advanced the Lost Cause with a book trilogy glorifying this organization that was adapted into the film Birth of a Nation. Nathan Bedford Forrest founded this white supremacist organization.
parts.answer: Ku Klux Klan [or the KKK; prompt on the Klan]

parts.label: L
parts.question: In a story by this author, Eddie shows the poem “Why Must it Always Be Tomato Soup?” to Bertha Young, who is continually overcome with the title emotion. For 10 points each:

parts.label: A
parts.question: [H] Name this author of the story “Bliss,” who described Laura breaking down and repeating “isn’t life—” after she delivers a basket of leftovers to the late Mr. Scott’s house in another story.

parts.label: B
parts.question: [E] Mansfield was from this country. In her story “How Pearl Button Was Kidnapped,” she describes two women belonging to this country’s indigenous Māori population taking a little girl to the sea for the first time.

parts.label: C
parts.question: [M] Mansfield wrote her story “Prelude” after this author asked her for material for the Hogarth Press. The title character sleeps with Elizabeth I and wakes up as a woman in this author’s novel Orlando: A Biography.

parts.label: L
parts.question: In one experiment, Schachter and Singer injected participants with a false drug called Suproxin to test a two-factor theory of these things. For 10 points each:

parts.label: A
parts.question: [H] Name these things that were found to depend on environmental cues, causing people to misattribute and mislabel them. Alexithymia [uh-LEX-ih-THY-mee-uh] is the inability to identify these things.

parts.label: B
parts.question: [E] In one study, participants were more likely to find a woman attractive if they met her while walking across a suspension bridge because of the misattribution of this emotion. Horror movies tend to cause this emotion.

parts.label: C
parts.question: [M] Some researchers believe that a “normative” type of alexithymia appears more often in these people. A “toxic” form of a certain trait can cause these people to be more susceptible to depression and substance abuse.
parts.answer: males [or men; accept word forms such as being a man; prompt on toxic masculinity]

parts.label: L
parts.question: In the 2010s, this manufacturer’s Formula One team was sponsored by Mission Winnow, a shell corporation created by Phillip Morris to dodge bans on tobacco advertising. For 10 points each:

parts.label: A
parts.question: [E] Name this Italian sports car manufacturer whose logo features a prancing horse. Ford’s attempt to defeat this manufacturer at the 1966 24 Hours of Le Mans was chronicled in a 2019 film starring Matt Damon.
parts.answer: Ferrari [accept Scuderia Ferrari or Ford v Ferrari]

parts.label: B
parts.question: [M] Recent Formula One seasons have featured title battles between Ferrari and this German constructor, which Lewis Hamilton won six championships driving for. This manufacturer’s teams are nicknamed the “silver arrows.”

parts.label: C
parts.question: [H] Between 2010 and 2014, this Spanish driver drove for Ferrari, having previously won two championships with Renault [renn-oh]. This driver has entered the Indianapolis 500 three times, shockingly failing to qualify in 2019.

parts.label: L
parts.question: In 1998, Aretha Franklin stepped in to perform this aria after its original performer was too sick. For 10 points each:

parts.label: A
parts.question: [H] Name this aria delivered by Prince Calaf about a princess who has three riddles. This aria ends with the word “Vincerò” sustained on B then up a note to A.

parts.label: B
parts.question: [E] “Nessun Dorma” appears in Turandot, an opera by this composer of La Bohème and Madame Butterfly.

parts.label: C
parts.question: [M] This opera singer’s last performance was “Nessun Dorma.” This singer was nicknamed for his ability to handle the high C’s in La Fille du Regiment and formed the Three Tenors with Placido Domingo and José Carreras.

parts.label: L
parts.question: Answer the following about damnatio memoriae, or the literal erasure of public figures in ancient Rome. For 10 points each:

parts.label: A
parts.question: [M] Erasing the memories of people sometimes meant re-arranging homes to disrupt the technique of “memory palaces” illustrated by this man in De Oratore. Mark Antony’s wife Fulvia stabbed the tongue of this master orator.

parts.label: B
parts.question: [E] Erasing the images of governors or emperors was often difficult because they appeared on these objects like the denarius or libra. These objects were commonly minted in silver and used to purchase in Roman forums.

parts.label: C
parts.question: [H] After burying the Vestal Virgin Cornelia alive amongst other cruel acts, this dynasty’s last member Domitian was subject to a damnatio memoriae. This dynasty arose under Vespasian after the Year of the Four Emperors.

parts.label: L
parts.question: For 10 points each, answer the following about antimatter:

parts.label: A
parts.question: [E] Compared to ordinary matter, antimatter particles have the opposite value of this quantity measured in coulombs.

parts.label: B
parts.question: [M] This antimatter particle, whose charge is plus-one, is the counterpart to an electron. One of these particles is emitted in beta-plus decay.

parts.label: C
parts.question: [H] Antimatter was first imagined by this physicist, who thought of positrons as “holes” in a space-filling “sea” of neutral particles. This Englishman’s namesake equation describes the wavefunction of spin one-half particles.
parts.answer: Paul Dirac [dih-RAK] [accept Dirac sea or Dirac equation]

parts.label: L
parts.question: In one poem, this poet described a girl who “befriended a stranded star whose rays five languid fingers were.” For 10 points each:

parts.label: A
parts.question: [M] Name this poet who wrote about “maggie and milly and molly and may” in one poem. Another work by this poet describes how “anyone lived in a pretty how town… with up so floating many bells down.”

parts.label: B
parts.question: [H] In “maggie and milly and molly and may,” “may [comes] home with a smooth round stone as small as a world and as large as alone” from this place. The poem ends with the line “it’s always ourselves we find in [this place].”
parts.answer: the sea [or the ocean; accept the beach or shoreline or coast]

parts.label: C
parts.question: [E] cummings largely did not use letters with this property in his poems, including in the names of maggie, milly, molly, and may. The first letter of a sentence or a name generally has this property.
parts.answer: capitalized letters [or uppercase letters or capitalization]

parts.label: L
parts.question: For 10 points each, answer the following about Ino [AI-no], a legendary queen of Boeotia [bee-OH-schuh] who was transformed into the goddess Leucothea [lay-co-THEE-ah] after jumping into the sea:

parts.label: A
parts.question: [M] Ino was the daughter of Harmonia and this founder of Thebes. This hero earned the ire of Ares after killing a sacred dragon and sowing its teeth.

parts.label: B
parts.question: [E] Ino appears to this hero and guides him to the island of Corfu. This hero struggles to return home to Ithaca and his wife Penelope after the Trojan War.

parts.label: C
parts.question: [H] Ino is said to be the ancestor of several members of this group. The rituals of this group often climaxed with the rites of sparagmos [spah-rag-moes] and omophagia [oh-moe-fah-gee-ah], or tearing apart a living thing and eating its flesh raw.
parts.answer: maenads [or Bacchae or Bassarids or Bacchantes; prompt on Thiasus]

parts.label: L
parts.question: Answer the following about the ultra-diffuse galaxy NGC 1052-DF2 [N-G-C one-oh-five-two D-F-two], for 10 points each:

parts.label: A
parts.question: [E] Like all ultra-diffuse galaxies, DF2 has an extremely low luminosity and thus emits very little of this phenomenon, which is carried by photons.

parts.label: B
parts.question: [M] DF2 is a candidate for the first known galaxy with none of this substance. Vera Rubin found evidence for this substance from its gravitational effect on galaxy rotation curves.

parts.label: C
parts.question: [H] DF2 is also known for having an extremely luminous population of these large, spherical star clusters that are rich in Population II [two] stars.

parts.label: L
parts.question: Answer the following about Ostalgie [OHSS-tal-gee], for 10 points each:

parts.label: A
parts.question: [M] Ostalgie is nostalgia for things made in this country. The “chemical breakdown” tactics of psychological torture were used by this country’s Stasi secret police.
parts.answer: East Germany [or German Democratic Republic; or GDR; or Deutsche Demokratische Republik; or DDR; reject “West Germany”; reject “Federal Republic of Germany”; reject “Germany” alone]

parts.label: B
parts.question: [E] Ostalgie includes a fondness for one of these products called Vita. In Nazi Germany, a formula for this product called Fanta was created after a trade embargo with Coke.

parts.label: C
parts.question: [H] A caricature of this leader in a straw hat appeared on East German traffic lights and is appreciated by Ostalgie enjoyers. This last head of state of East Germany was depicted kissing Leonid Brezhnev in a Berlin Wall mural.

parts.label: L
parts.question: You're trying to emulate a violin. For 10 points each:

parts.label: A
parts.question: [H] You might use this flexible electronic instrument championed by Wendy Carlos that creates waveforms and uses filters and envelopes to change its characteristics.
parts.answer: synthesizer [accept specific types of synthesizers such as analog synthesizer or Moog synthesizer]

parts.label: B
parts.question: [E] Like violins, most synthesizers are able to produce sounds with varying levels of this property. This property related to frequency determines how "low" or "high" a sound is.

parts.label: C
parts.question: [M] You might use low-frequency oscillations to emulate this effect on a synthesizer. Violinists create this pulsating change in pitch by wobbling their fingers from side to side.

parts.label: L
parts.question: Influencer “hauls” from brands that follow this business model have been criticized for promoting waste. For 10 points each:

parts.label: A
parts.question: [M] Name this business model, in which trendy clothing styles are mass-produced and cycled rapidly through retail stores. Brands that follow this business model include Zara and H&M.

parts.label: B
parts.question: [H] Diane von Fürstenberg, Gwen Stefani, and Anna Sui are among the many designers that have sued this fast fashion brand for copying their designs. This brand gives customers bright yellow plastic bags with John 3:16 printed on the bottom.

parts.label: C
parts.question: [E] Alternatives to partaking in fast fashion include shopping at these stores that recycle donated clothes. Examples of these stores include Salvation Army and Goodwill.
parts.answer: thrift stores [or thrift shops; or charity shops; or opportunity shops]

parts.label: L
parts.question: This character requires that any two eggs he eats must be of equal size. For 10 points each:

parts.label: A
parts.question: [H] Name this man, who refers to his intelligence as his “little grey cells.” In one novel, this character unknowingly encounters the gangster Lanfranco Cassetti.

parts.label: B
parts.question: [M] In this novel, Poirot solves a murder while stranded in Croatia due to a snowdrift. In this novel, it is determined that all twelve possible suspects in the stabbing of Samuel Ratchett committed the crime.

parts.label: C
parts.question: [E] Murder on the Orient Express is a crime novel by this English writer. This prolific murder mystery author also created Miss Marple.
parts.answer: Agatha Christie [or Agatha Mary Clarissa Christie; accept Agatha Mary Clarissa Miller]

parts.label: L
parts.question: Answer the following about electrolysis, for 10 points each:

parts.label: A
parts.question: [M] In contrast to a galvanic cell, an electrolytic cell requires energy to be inputted because the change in this quantity is greater than zero, meaning the reaction is not spontaneous.
parts.answer: Gibbs free energy [prompt on delta G]

parts.label: B
parts.question: [E] The Caster-Kellner process uses electrolysis to isolate sodium and chlorine from salt water, using a cathode of this metal that is liquid at room temperature.

parts.label: C
parts.question: [H] This English scientist pioneered the use of electrolysis to isolate various metals. This man discovered sodium, potassium, and calcium, among other elements.

parts.label: L
parts.question: Freddie Mercury was born to a Farsi family living on this archipelago. For 10 points each:

parts.label: A
parts.question: [M] Name this archipelago where the spice trade center of Stone Town can be found on Unguja island. This archipelago’s House of Wonders was a palace where Omani sultans ruled over the coast of modern-day Tanzania.

parts.label: B
parts.question: [E] Down the coast from Zanzibar is this island home to the Malagasy people and the lemur. The Avenue of the Baobabs is also located in this country, which is across the Mozambique Channel from mainland Africa.
parts.answer: Madagascar [or Republic of Madagascar or Republique de Madagascar or Repoblikan'i Madagasikara]

parts.label: C
parts.question: [H] A flaperon from Malaysian Airlines Flight 370 was found on this island, around 400 miles east of Madagascar. This French overseas territory with its capital of Saint-Denis is located near Mauritius.

parts.label: L
parts.question: Answer the following about Marshal Phibun, for 10 points each:

parts.label: A
parts.question: [E] After a 1932 coup in which Phibun came to power in this country governed from Bangkok, he changed its official name from Siam to a name meaning “land of the free.”
parts.answer: Thailand [or Kingdom of Thailand; or Ratcha-anachak Thai]

parts.label: B
parts.question: [H] After a failed monarchist revolt, Phibun installed to the throne a boy studying in Switzerland, Ananda Mahidol, who then gained this regnal name. The current king of Thailand also has this regnal name.
parts.answer: Rama [accept Rama VIII; accept Rama X]

parts.label: C
parts.question: [M] During World War II, Phibun negotiated an alliance with this country, allowing its troops to pass through Thailand during the Burma Campaign.
parts.answer: Japan [or Nihon-koku; or Nippon-koku; or Empire of Japan; or Dai Nippon Teikoku; or Japanese Empire]

parts.label: L
parts.question: Maria Headley translated this word as “Bro!”, describing its speaker as a man in a bar “pounding a glass and demanding another.” For 10 points each:

parts.label: A
parts.question: [H] Name this Old English word. It opens a work that describes the “Spear-Danes in days gone by.”

parts.label: B
parts.question: [E] Seamus Heaney, an author from this country, translated “Hwæt!” as “So!” in his version of Beowulf. Jonathan Swift suggested that residents of this island eat their babies amidst a famine that preceded a potato blight.
parts.answer: Ireland [or Republic of Ireland or Eire]

parts.label: C
parts.question: [M] This author described “Hwæt!” as “a note ‘striking up’ at the beginning of a poem” and translated it as “Lo!” This author of The Silmarillion gave the lecture “Beowulf: the Monsters and the Critics.”
parts.answer: J.R.R. Tolkien [or John Ronald Reuel Tolkien]

parts.label: L
parts.question: Answer the following about the French Revolutionary Calendar, for 10 points each:

parts.label: A
parts.question: [H] Holidays celebrating Talent and Labor after the end of Fructidor were named for this umbrella term for lower-class French revolutionaries who wore trousers instead of bourgeois knee-britches.

parts.label: B
parts.question: [M] This summer month of the calendar names an event in which the Directory usurped the power of the Committee of Public Safety and Maximilien Robespierre, thus ending the Reign of Terror.

parts.label: C
parts.question: [E] The decimalized calendar was introduced to weaken the power of the Catholic Church by replacing this other calendar, the most widely used today. This calendar named for a pope replaced the Julian calendar.

parts.label: L
parts.question: Along the Loango Coast of the Kongo Kingdom, “scepter-slates” called lusumu made of this material were used by elders for storytelling. For 10 points each:

parts.label: A
parts.question: [E] Name this material used to create Chinese puzzle balls. This material is harvested from the tusks of elephants.

parts.label: B
parts.question: [H] An ivory head of Queen Esigie was one of the thousands of artworks looted from this African kingdom in the 1800s. Brass plates depicting obas of this kingdom make up its namesake “bronzes” at the British Museum.

parts.label: B
parts.question: [M] Charles IV imported Murano artisans to kickstart this city’s industry of “forest glass.” The Hussite Wars and the Thirty Years’ War both began with people being thrown out of windows in this city.
parts.answer: ANSWER: Prague [or Praha; accept Defenestrations of Prague]

parts.label: C
parts.question: [E] George Ravenscroft mass-produced crystal glasses made with this element instead of calcium. Historians believe trace amounts of this element in pipes, paint, and other household goods is a historical cause of mental disabilities.
parts.answer: ANSWER: lead [or lead crystal glass; accept Pb]

parts.label: L
parts.question: For 10 points each, answer the following about fountains in modern art:

parts.label: A
parts.question: [E] Constructivist sculptor Naum Gabo designed Revolving Torsion, a fountain located on the grounds of St. Thomas’ Hospital in this city. Two fountains flank Nelson’s Column in this city’s Trafalgar Square.

parts.label: B
parts.question: [M] Marcel Duchamp’s Fountain consists of an ordinary urinal displayed as art. The everyday nature of the urinal is typical of this series of Duchamp works, other examples of which include Prelude to a Broken Arm.

parts.label: C
parts.question: [H] Alexander Calder designed a fountain flowing with mercury for display at a 1937 exhibition of this painting. In 1974, Tony Shafrazi vandalized this painting with spray paint in protest of William Calley’s release from prison.

parts.label: L
parts.question: You are a TA catching cheaters in a computer science class. For 10 points each:

parts.label: A
parts.question: [E] You sigh as you see multiple assignments with identical code, but with different names given to these storage units of data. These things may have to be declared before standing in for a value.

parts.label: B
parts.question: [M] A few students use their real names as they post problems to a programming help site named for this occurrence. Infinite recursion often causes this occurrence in which memory is exceeded, leading to a crash.

parts.label: C
parts.question: [H] You easily catch cheaters using MOSS, a script compatible with this Bell Labs-created operating system. C was developed for this operating system that has a philosophy of easy-to-understand, accessible code.

parts.label: L
parts.question: One of these works describes how the title concept “dwells with… Joy, whose hand is ever at his lips.” For 10 points each:

parts.label: A
parts.question: [H] Name these works, one of which urges the reader to “go not to Lethe [“LEE-thee”].” Another of these works asks “what pipes and timbrels? What wild ecstasy?”

parts.label: B
parts.question: [M] This ode by John Keats describes how Ruth “stood in tears amid the alien corn.” In this poem, the narrator tells the title “light-winged Dryad of the trees” that “thou wast not born for death.”
parts.answer: ANSWER: “Ode to a Nightingale” [reject “Ode on a Nightingale”]

parts.label: C
parts.question: [E] In his “Ode to Melancholy,” Keats writes that melancholy “dwells with [this concept]--[this concept] that must die.” In his “Ode on a Grecian Urn,” Keats equates this concept, which is studied in aesthetics, to truth.

parts.label: L
parts.question: Venustiano Carranza rejected an offer laid out in this document. For 10 points each:

parts.label: A
parts.question: [H] Name this document, proposing a secret alliance between Germany and Mexico. This document was intercepted and decoded by Nigel de Grey and William Reginald Hall in Room 40.
parts.answer: ANSWER: Zimmermann Telegram [or Zimmermann Note or Zimmermann Cable]

parts.label: B
parts.question: [M] Two years prior, German U-boats sank the Lusitania, which caused this Secretary of State to resign. This former populist presidential candidate claimed “you shall not crucify mankind” upon the title object in one speech.

parts.label: C
parts.question: [E] This president, despite his slogan “he kept us out of war,” entered World War I in 1917. This president gave the Fourteen Points speech.

parts.label: L
parts.question: A test involving two of these objects and a hidden marble tests children’s ability to attribute false beliefs to others. For 10 points each:

parts.label: A
parts.question: [H] Name these objects used in the Sally-Anne test. In one experiment, children imitated behavior towards these objects such as verbally berating them or hitting them with mallets.

parts.label: B
parts.question: [E] In the first experiment using the Sally-Anne test, 80 percent of children with this condition were unable to understand Sally’s perspective. Difficulties with social interactions characterize this “spectrum disorder.”
parts.answer: ANSWER: autism spectrum disorder [or ASD; accept Asperger’s syndrome]

parts.label: C
parts.question: [M] The first Sally-Anne experiment also involved people with this condition, 86% of whom passed the test. This condition is caused by a triple copy of chromosome 21.

parts.label: L
parts.question: Answer the following about yellow ribbons in history, for 10 points each:

parts.label: A
parts.question: [H] Hundreds of yellow ribbons were used in demonstrations in the People Power Revolution, which removed this leader. This man was accused of having senator Ninoy Aquino assassinated.
parts.answer: Ferdinand Marcos [or Ferdinand Emmanuel Edralin Marcos Sr.]

parts.label: B
parts.question: [M] Canada launched Operation Yellow Ribbon in response to this event, which inspired the musical Come From Away. The town of Gander in Newfoundland housed many people stranded in this event.

parts.label: C
parts.question: [E] Victims of the Sewol ferry disaster in this country are commemorated with yellow ribbons. The Miracle on the Han River refers to massive growth in this country’s capital of Seoul.
parts.answer: South Korea [or the Republic of Korea; or ROK; prompt on Korea; reject “North Korea” or the “Democratic People’s Republic of Korea”]

parts.label: L
parts.question: Slater’s rules are used to calculate the effective nuclear charge on the Allred-Rochow scale, which measures this quantity. For 10 points each:

parts.label: A
parts.question: [H] Name this quantity for an atom, whose “equalization” was proposed by R. T. Sanderson.
parts.answer: electronegativity [accept word forms; accept Allred–Rochow electronegativity; accept electronegativity equalization]

parts.label: B
parts.question: [M] Another scale to measure electronegativity named for this scientist ranks elements from zero to four. Irwin Stone introduced this scientist to the idea that big doses of vitamin C can cure a cold.
parts.answer: Linus Pauling [or Linus Carl Pauling; accept Pauling scale]

parts.label: C
parts.question: [E] On the Pauling scale, this element, with symbol F, has the highest value of electronegativity. This element’s anion may be added to water supplies to help prevent tooth decay.

parts.label: L
parts.question: The novel Anne of Green Gables is set in this province's city of Avonlea. For 10 points each:

parts.label: A
parts.question: [H] Name this province connected to New Brunswick by the Confederation Bridge. The capital of this smallest province of Canada is Charlottetown.
parts.answer: Prince Edward Island [or Île-du-Prince-Édouard; accept PEI]

parts.label: B
parts.question: [M] By contrast, this other island in Nunavut is the largest in Canada. Most of the mountains on this island are named after Norse deities, including its tallest, Mount Odin.

parts.label: C
parts.question: [E] Another island in Canada, Vancouver Island, is home to Victoria, the capital of this westernmost Canadian province that borders the state of Washington.

parts.label: L
parts.question: This author thinks “It’s more real to me here than if I went up” while outside the Paris apartment of his former lover. For 10 points each:

parts.label: A
parts.question: [H] Name this New York socialite who questions his recent engagement to May Welland after seeing Ellen Olenska during a performance of Faust in the novel The Age of Innocence.

parts.label: B
parts.question: [E] This author’s autobiography A Backwards Glance revealed that Newland Archer was inspired by her own time with “old money” in New York. She wrote the Age of Innocence and Ethan Frome.

parts.label: C
parts.question: [M] Daniel Day-Lewis walked with a cane on and off the set of Martin Scorcese’s adaptation of The Age of Innocence as part of this acting technique developed by Konstantin Stanislavski in which actors try to embody their characters’ memories and motivations by acting exactly like them.

parts.label: L
parts.question: Some stories describe the origins of this activity as the volcano goddess Pele performing it to celebrate finding land in spite of Namakaokahaʻi [“nah-mah-koh-KAH-ah-ee”]. For 10 points each:

parts.label: A
parts.question: [M] Name this activity whose ku’i genre involves oli chants. Performers of this activity wear kī leaf dresses and lei.
parts.answer: hula dancing [prompt on dancing with “What type of dancing?”]

parts.label: B
parts.question: [H] Pele sends Hi’iaka [“hee-ah-ka”] on a journey to Kawai’i to find a husband after being awoken by these jula instruments. Griots of West Africa sing mythical stories while playing one of these instruments called the djembe.

parts.label: C
parts.question: [E] Hula dancing is a tradition in this archipelago, which was raised from the sea by Māui’s fish hook.

parts.label: L
parts.question: A king of this name was accused of having love affairs with a group of men known as les mignons [lay min-yohn]. For 10 points each:

parts.label: A
parts.question: [M] A Catholic king of France with what name fought a three-way war against a Duke of Guise [geez] and a king of Navarre [nuh-var] who also had this name?
parts.answer: Henry or Henri [awn-ree] [accept War of the Three Henrys; accept Henry III; accept Henry I, Duke of Guise; accept Henry IV or Good King Henry or Henry I of Navarre]

parts.label: B
parts.question: [E] The war began because Henry III did not want Henry of Navarre, who belonged to this religious sect, to be his heir. French members of this sect were known as Huguenots.
parts.answer: Protestants [or Protestantism; accept Calvinists or Calvinism]

parts.label: C
parts.question: [H] After winning the war, Henry of Navarre became Henry IV and converted to Catholicism to secure his rule over France, which he reportedly justified with this statement.
parts.answer: “Paris is well worth a mass” [or “Paris vaut bien une messe”]

parts.label: L
parts.question: For 10 points each, answer the following about the self, or Atman [AHT-mun], in Hindu philosophy:

parts.label: A
parts.question: [E] Along with the closely related samkhya [SAM-kyuh] school, this school of Hindu philosophy believed that the self was the soul. In the West, this school shares its name with a system of exercise based on meditation and poses.
parts.answer: yoga [accept laya yoga or kundalini yoga or raja yoga or bhakti yoga or karma yoga or jnana yoga]

parts.label: B
parts.question: [H] Like many Hindu schools of thought, the Charvaka school rejects the existence of the self, while also espousing this position. The term nāstika [NAH-stih-kuh] is often mistranslated as referring to this heterodox view.
parts.answer: atheism [accept descriptive answers like not believing in God; prompt on “materialism”] (It’s unclear what the most correct English translation of nāstika is, but common translations include “heterodox,” “not existent,” “heretic,” or even “no-self.”)

parts.label: C
parts.question: [M] The existence of the self is affirmed by āstika thinkers, as they accept the authority of these ancient Hindu scriptures. The Rig is the longest text in this collection of four Sanskrit sacred works.

parts.label: L
parts.question: This composer dedicated a song cycle based on poems by Friedrich Rückert to his dead daughter, Maria. For 10 points each:

parts.label: A
parts.question: [M] Name this Austrian composer of Songs on the Death of Children. He featured the tam-tam and the rute in his Tragic Symphony, which also contains three “hammer blows of fate.”

parts.label: B
parts.question: [H] The third “scherzo” movement of this Mahler piece heavily uses the pentatonic scale. This piece, which depicts the infinite beauty of nature, also includes a movement based on a poem called “The Solitary One in Autumn.”
parts.answer: Das Lied von der Erde [or The Song of the Earth]

parts.label: C
parts.question: [E] Mahler avoided naming The Song of the Earth as his symphony of this number to avoid a so-called "curse" of this number. Beethoven died after completing his symphony of this number, which includes a setting of Ode to Joy.
parts.answer: Ninth Symphony [or Symphony Number Nine; accept Beethoven’s Ninth; accept the Curse of the Ninth]

parts.label: L
parts.question: In the brain, the “parietal” one of these structures controls the phenomenon of graphesthesia, which is the ability to recognize writing on the skin purely through touch. For 10 points each:

parts.label: A
parts.question: [E] Name these parts of the cerebrum, which include temporal, frontal, and occipital examples.

parts.label: B
parts.question: [H] This part of the brain is responsible for relaying sensory information to the lobes through the cerebral cortex. A separate structure located under this part of the brain controls the pituitary gland and regulates body maintenance.

parts.label: C
parts.question: [M] The only sense that the thalamus does not relay information on is this sense, which is identified in the piriform cortex. Instead of being processed in the thalamus, information on this sense is sent to the olfactory bulb.

parts.label: L
parts.question: One character in this work survives because of his ability to repair shoes. For 10 points each:

parts.label: A
parts.question: [M] Name this book, in which the narrator’s father, Vladek, recounts his experiences in the Holocaust. In 2015, this Art Spiegelman book was removed from store shelves in Russia due to its use of a swastika on the cover.

parts.label: B
parts.question: [H] In Maus, nationalities are represented by various animals, with Polish people being this animal. In another novel, one of these animals and a human set down the Ace of Spades at the same time during a poker game.
parts.answer: pigs (The unnamed novel is Animal Farm.)

parts.label: C
parts.question: [E] Maus illustrates Vladek’s story in this medium. Examples of works in this medium, which combine words and images to tell a story, include the Amulet series and Persepolis.

parts.label: L
parts.question: Answer the following about the works of female performance artists, for 10 points each:

parts.label: A
parts.question: [E] Marina Abramovic's last performance with her partner Ulay, titled Lovers, involved walking from opposite ends of this structure. This 13,000-mile-long structure is not actually visible from space.
parts.answer: Great Wall of China [or Wànlǐ chángchéng]

parts.label: B
parts.question: [M] This performance artist allowed participants to cut off parts of her clothing in Cut Piece. This author of Grapefruit helped write the lyrics to her husband’s song “Imagine.”

parts.label: C
parts.question: [H] While more famous for her Infinity Mirror Room pieces, this artist often painted nude New Yorkers with polka dots. In Walking Piece, this artist walks through New York City in a brightly-colored kimono.

parts.label: L
parts.question: For 10 points each, answer the following about characters who die in fires:

parts.label: A
parts.question: [H] The “Ghosts of the Yellow Dog” are spirits of hobos who died in a boxcar fire in The Piano Lesson, a play set in this city. A different play set in this city’s protagonist has an affair with Alberta, who dies in childbirth.
parts.answer: Pittsburgh, Pennsylvania [accept The Pittsburgh Cycle] (The unnamed play is Fences.)

parts.label: B
parts.question: [M] In this author’s play Arcadia, Septimus Hodge waltzes with Thomasina Coverly, who dies when her dress catches fire. Another of this man’s plays sees two characters from Hamlet flip heads on a coin 92 times in a row.
parts.answer: Tom Stoppard [or Tomas Straussler] (The second play is Rosencrantz and Guildenstern are Dead.)

parts.label: C
parts.question: [E] In an Anton Chekov play, three characters with this relationship to each other save victims of a fire. In Macbeth, “weird” witches with this relation chant “Double, double, toil and trouble.”
parts.answer: sisters [accept siblings; accept Three Sisters; accept the Weird Sisters]

parts.label: L
parts.question: A massive stone at this location called the omphalos marked where two eagles released by Zeus met after circling the world. For 10 points each:

parts.label: A
parts.question: [M] Name this location where pilgrims would bathe in the Castalian Spring before offering donations like pies to a priestess named for the Python.

parts.label: B
parts.question: [E] The Oracle of Delphi was a priestess of this god who slew the Python. This twin brother of Artemis was the Greek god of music and archery.

parts.label: C
parts.question: [H] Delphi was on the slope of this mountain where Deucalion and Pyrrha’s ark washed up after a great flood. Mount Helicon or this mountain is identified as the home of the Muses.

parts.label: L
parts.question: Answer the following about signatures and their signers on the Declaration of Independence, for 10 points each:

parts.label: A
parts.question: [E] According to legend, this president of the Second Continental Congress made an absurdly large signature so that King George III could read it without his spectacles.

parts.label: B
parts.question: [H] An elaborate curve appears beneath this man’s signature, similar to the curves in the signatures of Silence Dogood and Richard Saunders. This man created the first American public library and fire station.

parts.label: C
parts.question: [M] Because he died in a 1777 duel, the rarest signature is this state’s first governor, Button Gwinnett. James Oglethorpe defended this colony during the War of Jenkin’s Ear.

parts.label: L
parts.question: This technique is generally slower than scan line techniques. For 10 points each,

parts.label: A
parts.question: [H] Name this technique that extrapolates light paths to generate images. It draws its name from a method in physics that models light by representing it as the namesake geometric object.
parts.answer: ray tracing [prompt on ray casting or path tracing or photon mapping]

parts.label: B
parts.question: [M] Increasing the number of rays when ray tracing can reduce this phenomenon that is the random variation of information. AM radios can create the “static” type of this phenomenon.

parts.label: C
parts.question: [E] Ray tracing can also trace the path of sound waves to create this physics phenomenon in which sound arrives after a delay. Shouting in a cave can produce this phenomenon.

parts.label: L
parts.question: Answer the following about Cuban involvement in African wars, for 10 points each:

parts.label: A
parts.question: [H] Cuban soldiers were sent in to fight for one of these two countries over their disputed region of Ogaden. These two countries were led by Siad Barre and Mengistu during the Ogaden War between them.
parts.answer: Somalia AND Ethiopia [accept answers in either order; accept Federal Republic of Somalia or Soomaaliya or Jamhuuriyadda Federaalkaa Soomaaliya for Somalia; accept Federal Democratic Republic of Ethiopia or Ityop’iya Federalawi Demokrasiyawi Ripeblik for Ethiopia; reject partial answers]

parts.label: B
parts.question: [M] Along with the Soviet Union, Cuba supported Samora Machel and his FRELIMO party in this country’s civil war. This country’s opposition party RENAMO wanted the AK-47 to be removed from its flag.
parts.answer: Mozambique [or Republic of Mozambique or Republica de Moçambique]

parts.label: C
parts.question: [E] Troops from this longtime Communist leader’s Cuba helped the MPLA in Angola’s Battle of Cuito Cuanavale.
parts.answer: Fidel Castro [or Fidel Alejandro Castro Ruz; prompt on Castro alone]

parts.label: L
parts.question: A character on this show vomits into a hot tub after another girl brags about being in a relationship with Nate Jacobs. For 10 points each:

parts.label: A
parts.question: [M] Name this HBO Show created by Sam Levinson. A fight erupts during a carousel scene in a play between Maddie and the Sydney Sweeney-played Cassie on this show.

parts.label: B
parts.question: [E] Euphoria stars this actress whose acting career started with the wildly different Disney Channel show Shake it Up. She played MJ in Spiderman: Homecoming.

parts.label: C
parts.question: [H] Zendaya also starred in this movie, playing the character Anne Wheeler who is the love interest of a playwright portrayed by Zac Efron. This movie contains the songs “Rewrite the Stars” and “A Million Dreams.”

parts.label: L
parts.question: Claude Monet depicted smoke billowing towards this location’s glass ceiling at the third Impressionist Exhibition. For 10 points each:

parts.label: A
parts.question: [H] Name this Parisian train station. A man jumps away from a ladder in a puddle in an Henri Cartier-Bresson [on-REE car-tee-YAY breh-SON] photograph titled “Behind [this building].”
parts.answer: Gare Saint-Lazare [accept Paris-Saint-Lazare; accept Behind the Gare Saint-Lazare]

parts.label: B
parts.question: [E] A child stares through a fence to the Gare Saint-Lazare in this artist’s painting The Railway. This artist of The Luncheon on the Grass depicted a Black servant gifting flowers to a reclining nude in his Olympia.

parts.label: C
parts.question: [M] This largest collection of Impressionist Art in the world occupies a former train station across the Seine from the Louvre. A gigantic Beaux-Arts [“boh-ZART”] clock overlooks this museum’s marble-white main room.

parts.label: L
parts.question: Answer the following about birthstones, for 10 points each:

parts.label: A
parts.question: [E] This gemstone is the birthstone for the month of May. This variant of the mineral beryl is green.

parts.label: B
parts.question: [M] Because the October birthstone, opal, is amorphous [ay-MOR-fuss], it is not one of these materials and is thus considered a mineraloid rather than a mineral. Types of these materials include isometric and monoclinic.
parts.answer: crystals [or crystalline solids; accept periodic materials]

parts.label: C
parts.question: [H] Ruby, the birthstone for July, gets its characteristic red color from the presence of this element. The trioxide of this element is typically purple, but turns orange when wet.

parts.label: L
parts.question: The epitaph of this poem describes “a youth to Fortune and Fame unknown.” For 10 points each:

parts.label: A
parts.question: [M] Name this poem that mourns “some Cromwell guiltless of his country's blood.” This poem begins with the line “the curfew tolls the knell of parting day.”

parts.label: B
parts.question: [H] The author of “Elegy Written in a Country Churchyard,” Thomas Gray, also wrote a poem describing the “angel forms” and “Tyrian hues” of these animals. In that poem, Selima “stretches in vain to reach” some of these animals.
parts.answer: goldfish [accept, but do NOT reveal “Ode on the Death of a Favourite Cat Drowned in a Tub of Goldfishes”; prompt on “fish”]

parts.label: C
parts.question: [E] That poem is titled for one of these events “of a Favorite Cat.” Elegies are poems that mourn these events.
parts.answer: deaths [accept “Ode on the Death of a Favourite Cat Drowned in a Tub of Goldfishes”; accept word forms like dying]

parts.label: L
parts.question: When Ra sent Hathor to punish humanity for conspiring against him, she transformed into this goddess and was only stopped when she drank 7,000 gallons of beer stained to resemble blood. For 10 points each:

parts.label: A
parts.question: [H] Name this “Lady of Terror,” an Egyptian goddess who defended Ma’at and had the head of a lioness.

parts.label: B
parts.question: [M] Sekhmet is one of many goddesses recognized as these body parts belonging to Ra. Thoth magically restored one of these body parts belonging to Horus called the wedjet.
parts.answer: ANSWER: eyes [accept Eye of Ra or Eye of Horus]

parts.label: C
parts.question: [E] Prayers to Sekhmet were whispered into the ears of cats who had undergone this process. Canopic jars contained organs that were removed from bodies before they were wrapped in bandages as part of this process.
parts.answer: ANSWER: mummification [accept descriptive answers such as turning into a mummy; prompt on embalming; prompt on burial; prompt on entombment; prompt on preservation; prompt on dying]

parts.label: L
parts.question: Harvey Fletcher helped run this experiment, in which an electric field was created below a chamber connected to a misting device. For 10 points each:

parts.label: A
parts.question: [M] Name this 1909 experiment in which electrons emitted from air ionized by x-rays attached to drops of a substance sprayed through an atomizer.
parts.answer: ANSWER: oil drop experiment [or the Millikan oil drop experiment; prompt on the Millikan experiment]

parts.label: B
parts.question: [E] The oil drop experiment determined that this value for an electron was about negative 1.6 times ten to the minus nineteenth coulombs. This value is negative for electrons, but positive for protons.

parts.label: C
parts.question: [H] To calculate the mass of the oil drop, Milliken and Fletcher accounted for drag using this law, which for objects with small Reynolds numbers, equates the drag force to six pi times viscosity times radius times flow velocity.

parts.label: L
parts.question: In 1979, the shock jock Steve Dahl lead a storming of a Chicago White Sox and Detroit Tigers game so that people could blow up CDs of this genre of music in the outfield. For 10 points each:

parts.label: A
parts.question: [E] Name this genre of music popular in the 1970s. The film Saturday Night Fever portrays afros, one-piece suits, and glittering “balls” over dancefloors as key elements of this genre.
parts.answer: ANSWER: disco music [accept disco balls; accept Disco Demolition Night]

parts.label: B
parts.question: [H] Disco hustles often featured swoops or “lateral” examples of this partner dance move, in which one partner lowers the other towards the ground.

parts.label: C
parts.question: [M] Dips in disco moves were inspired by this other dance. Astor Piazolla used the accordion-related instrument the bandoneón in his compositions for this dance that emerged in dance halls along the Río de la Plata.

parts.label: L
parts.question: During this man’s presidency, the Klondike Gold Rush helped stimulate investment and recover from the Panic of 1893. For 10 points each:

parts.label: A
parts.question: [E] Name this Democratic President, the only to hold two non-consecutive terms split by Benjamin Harrison.

parts.label: B
parts.question: [H] Despite being targeted with the phrase “Ma Ma, Where’s My Pa” over his affair with Maria Halpin, Cleveland won the 1884 election against this Republican who was nicknamed the “continental liar from the state of Maine.”

parts.label: C
parts.question: [M] Cleveland established Labor Day after this event in which Richard Olney leveraged federal intervention through the Sherman Antitrust Act. Eugene Debs and the ARU led this 1894 railroad strike in Illinois.

parts.label: L
parts.question: For 10 points each, answer the following about Ezra Pound’s literary career:

parts.label: A
parts.question: [H] Early in his career, Pound found success publishing in The English Review, an influential magazine published by this author. This author wrote the Parade’s End tetralogy and The Good Soldier.
parts.answer: ANSWER: Ford Madox Ford [or Ford Hermann Hueffer]

parts.label: B
parts.question: [M] After arguing over the direction of Imagism with a member of this family, Pound began referring to it as “Amygism.” Other members of this Boston-centered literary family include Robert, who wrote “Skunk Hour.”
parts.answer: ANSWER: Lowell family [accept Amy Lowell or Robert Lowell IV]

parts.label: C
parts.question: [E] Once Imagism had dissolved, Pound began agitating for this authoritarian political ideology in works like Jef erson and/or Mussolini, which supported the Blackshirts.

parts.label: L
parts.question: Answer the following about the chemistry of fireworks, for 10 points each:

parts.label: A
parts.question: [E] The rotten eggs smell of fireworks comes from this bright yellow element that appears below oxygen on the periodic table.

parts.label: B
parts.question: [H] Compounds with this property like potassium chloride are produced from sparkler smoke and can damage lungs. Deliquescent materials have this property, which means they attract and hold water.
parts.answer: ANSWER: hygroscopic [accept word forms like hygroscopy; reject “hydroscopic”]

parts.label: C
parts.question: [M] Lithium and this element are used to create red fireworks and also burn red during the flame test. This element’s isotope 90 is spread widely in nuclear fallout and can replace calcium in bones.

parts.label: L
parts.question: In a play written in this language, a beggar brawls with a Buddhist monk because he thinks he stole a bowl, only for it to later be discovered that the bowl was in fact stolen by a dog. For 10 points each:

parts.label: A
parts.question: [M] Name this language that the playwright Kālidāsa [kaa-lee-daa-suh] wrote in.
parts.answer: ANSWER: Sanskrit (The play in the leadin is A Farce of Drunken Sport by Pallava emperor Mahendravarman I.)

parts.label: B
parts.question: [H] Sanskrit was used to write adaptations of stories from the Mahabharata [mah-ha-BAH-ruh-tuh], including the tale of this wife of Dushyanta [doo-shyun-tah]. A Kālidāsa play retells the story of this character.
parts.answer: ANSWER: Shakuntala [accept The Sign of Shakuntala or The Recognition of Shakuntalam or The Sign of Shakuntalam or Abhijnanashakuntala or Abhijñāna Shākuntalam]

parts.label: C
parts.question: [E] Virtually every surviving classical Indian play has a happy ending, meaning that there are no Sanskrit plays that could be classified as this genre. Aristotle’s Poetics contrasts this genre with comedy.

parts.label: L
parts.question: Answer some questions about new national parks, for 10 points each:

parts.label: A
parts.question: [M] One of the last habitats of this state’s namesake “condor” is its Pinnacles National Park, which was established in 2013. This state has the most national parks, including Kings Canyon and Channel Islands.
parts.answer: ANSWER: California [or CA; accept California condor]
